The whole-block log surrogate is close to the NLL baseline in Table 2. This variant optimizes $\log r_{b}+\log S_{b}$ , rather than the raw importance-weighted quantity in Equation 14. When the drafter is still poor, $r_{b}=q(x_{1:b}\mid y)/p(x_{1:b}\mid y)$ is often very small, while the acceptance factors $A_{j}$ saturate near $1$ on target-sampled prefixes. Consequently, $S_{b}$ changes slowly and the gradient is dominated by $\log r_{b}$ , making the update resemble block NLL. Truncating low-overlap prefixes improves the training signal, and summing all retained prefixes gives the strongest result for both $K\!=\!1$ and $K\!=\!4$ .
5 Related Work
Speculative decoding and speculative sampling.
Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by proposing tokens with a cheap draft model and verifying them with the target model (Leviathan et al. 2023). Speculative sampling extends the same principle to stochastic decoding while preserving the target distribution (Chen et al. 2023). Most analyses and systems focus on improving draft accuracy or target-model verification efficiency. Our work focuses on a different failure mode: when the drafter proposes an entire block non-autoregressively, the block’s joint structure can matter as much as the marginal accuracy of individual positions.
Parallel and block drafters.
Multi-token prediction and block drafting reduce the number of target-model invocations by proposing several future tokens per pass (Gloeckle et al. 2024; Cai et al. 2024). DFlash uses a block diffusion drafter to generate draft tokens efficiently and is especially effective for greedy speculative decoding (Chen et al. 2026). D-PACE changes the training objective for parallel speculative drafters by assigning dynamic position-aware cross-entropy weights (Wu et al. 2026). Other draft-head methods introduce sequential or semi-autoregressive structure inside the draft, including Hydra, EAGLE, and DSpark (Ankner et al. 2024; Li et al. 2024; Cheng et al. 2026). These methods improve drafting quality, but they either retain independent block sampling or introduce within-draft serialization. Our focus is the conditional mismatch introduced by independent non-autoregressive block sampling under non-greedy verification.
Dependent multi-token modeling.
Recent tensor-decomposition and probabilistic-circuit approaches to multi-token prediction show that explicitly modeling dependencies among future positions can improve the expressiveness of parallel predictors (Basharin et al. 2025; Grivas et al. 2026). These methods typically train by maximizing the likelihood of a target future block under the proposal distribution. For a factorized proposal, this reduces to the standard sum of per-position cross-entropies; for a CP-style latent-mixture proposal, it becomes a marginalized block negative log-likelihood that distributes credit across latent branches according to the learned prior. We use these objectives as likelihood baselines for both independent and dependent drafters.
6 Limitations
The current study establishes the draft proposal quality benefits of both dependent block drafting and acceptance-oriented training, while leaving three directions for further investigation.
Effect of training data stochasticity
We primarily evaluated the drafters trained with a set of target responses that are generated using the default sampling parameters. However, inherently, dependent modeling may benefit from more stochasticity in training target blocks since the drafter is exposed to a more accurate representation of target block distribution. We leave the exploration of training dataset stochasticity to future work.
Acceptance-oriented objective.
We optimize a threshold-truncated, log-domain surrogate motivated by expected accepted length.
The surrogate is designed to provide a practical training signal when drafter–target overlap is limited,
and our experiments show that it consistently improves accepted length.
It does not,
however,
provide the formal guarantees of an unbiased estimator or lower bound,
leaving tighter acceptance-aligned objectives as an interesting direction for future work.
Training and inference proposals.
Training uses the differentiable soft latent-mixture proposal,
whereas our primary evaluation samples a category and greedily decodes its corresponding branch.
This design enables differentiable training while retaining efficient block decoding at inference,
and its consistent gains across models,
tasks,
and sampling regimes demonstrate effective empirical transfer.
A formal characterization of the relationship between the soft training distribution and the resulting greedy-branch proposal remains open.
7 Conclusion
We studied block diffusion drafters for non-greedy speculative decoding and showed that independent block sampling creates a fundamental mismatch in non-greedy speculative decoding:
the drafter predicts future positions separately,
while the target verifies them conditionally in a sequential manner.
We show that this mismatch becomes increasingly costly as target decoding grows more stochastic,
causing independently sampled blocks to lose acceptance precisely when multiple continuations are plausible.
To address this limitation, we introduced DBlast, a dependent block drafter that represents coherent block-level alternatives through a low-rank latent mixture and trains them with an acceptance-oriented objective aligned with sequential verification.
DBlast preserves efficient one-pass parallel drafting while consistently improving accepted length across math, coding, chat, and creative-writing tasks,
with a $12.1\%$ macro-average gain for Qwen3-8B in the highest-entropy setting.
These results demonstrate that within-block dependency modeling and acceptance-aligned training are complementary ingredients for efficient stochastic speculative decoding.

Appendix A Supplementary Material This supplement provides the technical and experimental details supporting the main paper. Section B provides DBLast overall design and specifies the proposal used by the reported greedy-branch decoder and its exact verification. Section C documents the early-determinism diagnosis. Section D investigates the latency overhead of adding dependency to the drafter, Section E gives the full training configuration, and finally Section F covers qualitative behavior of DBLast. Appendix B DBLast Drafting and Verification Figure 3 illustrates the overall implementation of low-rank mixture dependency modeling in DBLast. Inputs are target prefix hidden states, anchor and masked tokens. The DFlash backbone computes the shared block hidden states; the category-prior head defines the category distribution; and the hidden expander computes all category-specific hidden states in parallel. The category distribution and the branch token distributions define the dependent draft proposal. 66	Abstract
67	Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by drafting future
68	tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. A diffusion-style drafter, such as DFlash,
69	drafts an entire block in one forward pass. It is trained on the per-position marginals rather than
70	on the joint distribution over the block, so the tokens it emits are individually plausible yet
71	jointly incoherent. We introduce LiLiCorr, a Lightweight Likelihood-based model that
72	Correlates the per-position marginal distributions such a drafter produces.
73	It keeps the top- $K$ tokens at each position as candidates and processes them
74	jointly, producing for each an in and an out vector. A pair at consecutive positions matches
75	when the earlier candidate’s out vector aligns, in cosine similarity, with the later one’s
76	in vector. Training makes the correct pairings score highest while pushing
77	competing ones down, so coherent blocks outscore incoherent ones. The joint distribution over the
78	block, exponential in its length, is never materialized. One lightweight network
79	pass produces all the vectors, and the pairwise scores follow as batched matrix operations,
80	leaving only a cheap greedy walk sequential. We
81	co-train the DFlash drafter with LiLiCorr, so it learns to propose
82	candidates that correlate into longer accepted sequences. Over the vanilla DFlash drafter it builds on, LiLiCorr accepts more and serves faster at every one of the $72$ settings we
83	test: nine benchmarks at two target sizes under greedy and temperature-one decoding, together
84	with a throughput sweep over six concurrencies, two input lengths and three output-entropy tiers.
85	It raises acceptance length by $7$ to $19\%$ , while its
86	single-pass scoring head accounts for only about $3\%$ of the per-block latency. Against
87	three concurrently developed methods that also restore coherence at draft time, every system
88	equally optimized on a common serving stack, LiLiCorr holds the highest
89	throughput in $63$ of those settings, ties within a measured noise floor in $6$ , and trails in
90	only $3$ .
91	1 Introduction
92	Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive language-model inference by letting a
93	small draft model propose several future tokens that the target model verifies in
94	parallel, keeping the longest correct prefix (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023).
95	Because decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, verifying a multitude of tokens together costs
96	little more than generating just one token. The resulting speedup depends on two quantities: the
97	acceptance length, the expected number of draft tokens accepted per step, and
98	the cost of the drafter itself. A good drafter must raise the former without inflating
99	the latter. Much effort therefore goes into raising acceptance length, with designs
100	ranging from feature-autoregressive heads such as EAGLE
101	(Li et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2026) to multi-head predictors such as Medusa
102	(Cai et al., 2024). A particularly promising approach predicts an entire block of
103	future tokens in a single forward pass via a parallel diffusion-style drafter,
104	such as DFlash (Chen et al., 2026), offering a long speculative window at very low
105	cost.
106	In this work we build on DFlash, which predicts an entire block of future tokens in one forward
107	pass. For each position in the block, henceforth a slot, it produces a
108	distribution over the full vocabulary. Although DFlash attends bidirectionally across
109	slots, so its representations can in principle correlate different positions, it is
110	optimized with a per-position cross-entropy that supervises only the token
111	marginal at each slot. This leaves the joint distribution over the block
112	largely unconstrained, so DFlash predicts each slot well yet can assemble the tokens into an
113	incoherent block.
114	This marginals problem is well known in the discrete diffusion literature, and its
115	origin is combinatorial: the joint distribution over a block of $B$ positions, each
116	drawn from a vocabulary of size $V$ , has $V^{B}$ possible realizations, so
117	materializing it is intractable even for very short blocks. Diffusion language models
118	therefore never model the joint explicitly, and both diffusion and speculative-decoding literature offer ways to recover coherence without it. Masked
119	diffusion models such as LLaDA, MDLM, and Dream
120	(Nie et al., 2026; Sahoo et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025) correlate the sequence through iterative
121	denoising, re-masking a subset of the predicted tokens and re-predicting them over
122	several rounds. In a speculative-decoding setting, however, each such round is another
123	full drafter pass, which is too expensive. Tree-based reranking, such as DDTree
124	(Ringel and Romano, 2026), expands several candidate paths from the per-slot marginals and lets
125	the target model select among them. This shifts the correlation work onto the target,
126	whose passes speculative decoding is designed to save. The trade is especially
127	unfavorable in the compute-bound, high-concurrency regime typical of real-world
128	serving.
129	In contrast, Domino (Huang et al., 2026) and DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), two works concurrent
130	with ours, act at draft time while avoiding extra target passes, but
131	they do so through a sequence of auto-regressive neural-network passes, one on each draft slot.
132	A third work developed concurrently with ours, DFlash2 (Inco AI, 2026), avoids the
133	per-slot pass, scoring each adjacent pair of tokens from learned embeddings of their two identities.
134	Compatibility is therefore a property of the token pair itself rather than of the draft it appears
135	in: the same two tokens score alike in every context.

138	at each slot in one forward pass, and taking the most probable token of each slot independently
139	yields a sequence that is locally probable but jointly incoherent. (b) LiLiCorr retains the

145	We introduce LiLiCorr, a lightweight likelihood-based model that recovers a coherent
146	sequence from the per-slot marginals in a single network pass. Figure 1 sets out the method end to end. LiLiCorr takes the top- $K$ candidate tokens at each slot and produces two vectors per
147	candidate: in and out. These capture how candidates chain together: two

LiLiCorr: Lightweight Likelihood Correlation
of Parallel Drafts for Speculative Decoding
Matan Rusanovsky

Abstract
Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by drafting future
tokens that the target model verifies in parallel. A diffusion-style drafter, such as DFlash,
drafts an entire block in one forward pass. It is trained on the per-position marginals rather than
on the joint distribution over the block, so the tokens it emits are individually plausible yet
jointly incoherent. We introduce LiLiCorr, a Lightweight Likelihood-based model that
Correlates the per-position marginal distributions such a drafter produces.
It keeps the top- $K$ tokens at each position as candidates and processes them
jointly, producing for each an in and an out vector. A pair at consecutive positions matches
when the earlier candidate’s out vector aligns, in cosine similarity, with the later one’s
in vector. Training makes the correct pairings score highest while pushing
competing ones down, so coherent blocks outscore incoherent ones. The joint distribution over the
block, exponential in its length, is never materialized. One lightweight network
pass produces all the vectors, and the pairwise scores follow as batched matrix operations,
leaving only a cheap greedy walk sequential. We
co-train the DFlash drafter with LiLiCorr, so it learns to propose
candidates that correlate into longer accepted sequences. Over the vanilla DFlash drafter it builds on, LiLiCorr accepts more and serves faster at every one of the $72$ settings we
test: nine benchmarks at two target sizes under greedy and temperature-one decoding, together
with a throughput sweep over six concurrencies, two input lengths and three output-entropy tiers.
It raises acceptance length by $7$ to $19\%$ , while its
single-pass scoring head accounts for only about $3\%$ of the per-block latency. Against
three concurrently developed methods that also restore coherence at draft time, every system
equally optimized on a common serving stack, LiLiCorr holds the highest
throughput in $63$ of those settings, ties within a measured noise floor in $6$ , and trails in
only $3$ .
1 Introduction
Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive language-model inference by letting a
small draft model propose several future tokens that the target model verifies in
parallel, keeping the longest correct prefix (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023).
Because decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, verifying a multitude of tokens together costs
little more than generating just one token. The resulting speedup depends on two quantities: the
acceptance length, the expected number of draft tokens accepted per step, and
the cost of the drafter itself. A good drafter must raise the former without inflating
the latter. Much effort therefore goes into raising acceptance length, with designs
ranging from feature-autoregressive heads such as EAGLE
(Li et al., 2024a; Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2026) to multi-head predictors such as Medusa
(Cai et al., 2024). A particularly promising approach predicts an entire block of
future tokens in a single forward pass via a parallel diffusion-style drafter,
such as DFlash (Chen et al., 2026), offering a long speculative window at very low
cost.
In this work we build on DFlash, which predicts an entire block of future tokens in one forward
pass. For each position in the block, henceforth a slot, it produces a
distribution over the full vocabulary. Although DFlash attends bidirectionally across
slots, so its representations can in principle correlate different positions, it is
optimized with a per-position cross-entropy that supervises only the token
marginal at each slot. This leaves the joint distribution over the block
largely unconstrained, so DFlash predicts each slot well yet can assemble the tokens into an
incoherent block.
This marginals problem is well known in the discrete diffusion literature, and its
origin is combinatorial: the joint distribution over a block of $B$ positions, each
drawn from a vocabulary of size $V$ , has $V^{B}$ possible realizations, so
materializing it is intractable even for very short blocks. Diffusion language models
therefore never model the joint explicitly, and both diffusion and speculative-decoding literature offer ways to recover coherence without it. Masked
diffusion models such as LLaDA, MDLM, and Dream
(Nie et al., 2026; Sahoo et al., 2024; Ye et al., 2025) correlate the sequence through iterative
denoising, re-masking a subset of the predicted tokens and re-predicting them over
several rounds. In a speculative-decoding setting, however, each such round is another
full drafter pass, which is too expensive. Tree-based reranking, such as DDTree
(Ringel and Romano, 2026), expands several candidate paths from the per-slot marginals and lets
the target model select among them. This shifts the correlation work onto the target,
whose passes speculative decoding is designed to save. The trade is especially
unfavorable in the compute-bound, high-concurrency regime typical of real-world
serving.
In contrast, Domino (Huang et al., 2026) and DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), two works concurrent
with ours, act at draft time while avoiding extra target passes, but
they do so through a sequence of auto-regressive neural-network passes, one on each draft slot.
A third work developed concurrently with ours, DFlash2 (Inco AI, 2026), avoids the
per-slot pass, scoring each adjacent pair of tokens from learned embeddings of their two identities.
Compatibility is therefore a property of the token pair itself rather than of the draft it appears
in: the same two tokens score alike in every context.

sequence from the per-slot marginals in a single network pass. Figure 1 sets out the method end to end. LiLiCorr takes the top- $K$ candidate tokens at each slot and produces two vectors per
candidate: in and out. These capture how candidates chain together: two
adjacent candidates are compatible when the out vector of the first aligns, in
cosine similarity, with the in vector of the second. Training aligns the out
and in vectors of consecutive ground-truth tokens and separates the competing
pairings. At inference, a cheap greedy walk commits the block left to right,
at each position taking the candidate that best matches its committed predecessor. The novelty is that
every vector is produced in a single pass over all candidates at all slots, so each pair is scored
in the light of the candidates around it, at the slots before it and after it. Correlation then
reduces to matrix operations that are
easy to optimize, all candidate interactions computed in parallel, with only the greedy path
selection left sequential. Approaches that correct one slot at a time instead run their network at
every position.
LiLiCorr is trained jointly with DFlash rather than on top of a frozen drafter, so the
drafter learns to propose candidate sets that LiLiCorr can turn into longer accepted
sequences. Against a vanilla DFlash drafter trained on the same data, this raises
acceptance length by $7$ to $19\%$ on every benchmark, for 8B and 4B target sizes and both greedy and
temperature- $1$ decoding. We also compare against the three works above, Domino, DSpark
and DFlash2, which likewise tune the drafter alongside their head, giving
every system the same optimization effort on a common serving stack.
LiLiCorr is the fastest system at almost every setting we measure, and most of the few
exceptions sit inside the measurement noise. Against the two systems that correct one slot at a
time the advantage is structural, since they spend a network pass per slot where LiLiCorr scores
every candidate at once. Against DFlash2, which also drafts in one pass, the difference lies in the
scoring rule. DFlash2 scores a pair from the identities of its two tokens, so the same pair
scores alike in every draft, whereas every LiLiCorr score is formed from vectors that have seen
every candidate at every slot. This structural difference yields longer accepted prefixes, on
average at both target sizes and under both decoding regimes. The lead persists as
concurrency rises.
Contributions.
(1) 
A novel likelihood-based formulation of the marginals problem. We cast the recovery of a coherent sequence from per-slot marginals as a learned scoring model over candidate paths. Rather than reason in the full vocabulary, the model attends over all candidates of all slots by assigning two low-dimensional vectors to each, which encode how neighbors are matched.
(2) 
Correlation as efficient parallel matrix operations. At decoding time, a single
network pass precomputes all of the correlations, as the pairwise candidate interactions
reduce to matrix operations that are easy to optimize. This is followed by a cheap greedy walk that remains sequential.
(3) 
State-of-the-art results. LiLiCorr sets a new state-of-the-art for
draft-time correlation in speculative decoding, trained jointly with the drafter and given the same
data, training budget, and optimization effort as the three concurrent
works Huang et al. (2026); Cheng et al. (2026); Inco AI (2026). We evaluate on nine benchmarks, at two target sizes and under
both greedy and temperature-one decoding, and on a throughput sweep over six serving concurrencies,
two input lengths, and three output-entropy tiers. LiLiCorr holds the highest throughput of any
system compared in $63$ of these $72$ settings, ties within a measured noise floor in $6$ and
trails in only $3$ .

207	independent per-position predictions, so the sampled tokens are not guaranteed to be
208	jointly coherent. This is addressed via an iterative refinement, re-masking and re-predicting
209	subsets of tokens so that later rounds condition on earlier ones. Parallel drafters

211	full drafter pass, which negates the latency gains that motivate parallel drafting. Recovering

213	Recovering coherent drafts.
214	Several recent methods recover a coherent
215	sequence from the per-slot marginals that a parallel drafter such as DFlash produces.
216	One direction expands these
217	marginals into a draft tree of several continuations that the target verifies in a
218	single pass. DDTree (Ringel and Romano, 2026) is training-free, ranking candidate prefixes by
219	their marginal product, whereas Oda et al. (2026) first learn a small autoregressive
220	adapter before building the tree. Both push the correlation work onto the target,
221	spending the compute speculative decoding aims to save, and both rely on
222	tree-structured attention, which is typically less efficient than standard causal
223	attention. An alternative direction reintroduces the dependencies at draft time: Domino

225	condition each slot on the previously

248	3 Method
249	3.1 Setup: prefix acceptance and the marginal drafter
250	Let $M$ be a frozen target language model. A parallel block drafter proposes, in a
251	single forward pass, a block of $B$ positions conditioned on the verified
252	context, of which $B-1$ are future tokens. The first block position is the last token
253	the target has committed, which serves as the anchor, slot $0$ . The remaining $B-1$ positions are
254	the speculative slots $1,\dots,B-1$ . At each slot the drafter produces a distribution (logit) over the
255	vocabulary, a per-slot marginal. Standard decoding resolves each slot
256	independently, taking its most probable token. Once the draft is complete, the
257	target verifies the whole block in a single pass and accepts a prefix of it,
258	discarding everything from the first rejected position onward. With a greedy target a draft
259	token is accepted when it coincides with the target’s own choice. Under a sampling target,
260	acceptance instead follows the standard rejection test, which preserves the target distribution
261	exactly (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). In both regimes acceptance is
262	prefix-structured, and it is this structure that LiLiCorr is built around.
263	3.2 A scoring model over the candidate lattice
264	The drafter is supervised on per-slot marginals, so the tokens it selects are
265	individually probable but not necessarily compatible with one another. Selecting tokens
266	that are jointly compatible, and not only locally probable, can lengthen the accepted
267	prefix, and doing so at draft time could avoid extra target passes.
268	LiLiCorr addresses this goal by correlating the slots over a small pool of alternatives that the
269	drafter’s own marginal already places near the top. At each slot $s$ it retains the drafter’s
270	top- $K$ candidate tokens $c_{s,1},\dots,c_{s,K}$ rather than its single most probable
271	one. Each candidate is a token, and we represent it by a vector we call its node,
272	formed by summing four terms of equal width: the target’s frozen input embedding of the token, the
273	drafter’s hidden state at that slot, a small network over a few scalar features of how confident
274	the drafter is in that candidate, listed in Appendix A, and learned encodings of the
275	slot and of the candidate’s rank. The hidden state belongs to the slot and is shared by its $K$ 
276	candidates, so what separates them is the token itself, its confidence, and its rank. Across the
277	 $B-1$ slots these nodes form a $(B\!-\!1)\times K$ lattice.
278	A small Transformer processes the $(B\!-\!1)\times K$ nodes jointly. Its self-attention
279	lets every candidate exchange information with every other, both the competing candidates
280	within a slot and the candidates at neighboring slots, so each is represented in
281	the context of the whole block rather than on its own. Each attended node is then fused with a projection of the target’s hidden state that produced
282	the last verified token: the candidate’s own state, that projection, and their elementwise product
283	are concatenated and mapped back to the node width by a single layer. Though one vector common to
284	the whole block, it enters every candidate separately, so that the verifier’s view of the context,
285	and not the drafter’s alone, shapes each of them.
286	For each node LiLiCorr emits two
287	vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}$ , an out vector $\mathbf{o}$ and an in vector $\mathbf{i}$ , each
288	normalized to unit norm. The dimension $d_{e}$ is given in Appendix A. The anchor,
289	which precedes the first slot, is encoded far more thinly: the anchor projection itself, mapped by
290	its own head to one further out vector. Indexing the anchor as slot $0$ , we
291	write this vector $\mathbf{o}_{0}$ .
292	Adjacent slots $s$ and $s+1$ are then coupled by a single matching term, the cosine
293	similarity between the out and in vectors: | |$\phi^{\mathrm{p}}(s,k,k^{\prime})=\sigma\,\cossim(\mathbf{o}_{s,k},\,\mathbf{i}_{s+1,k^{\prime}})~~~~\mbox{for}~~~s=0,\dots,B-2,~~~1\leq k\leq K_{s},~1\leq k^{\prime}\leq K,$  | |(1)
294	where $\cossim(\cdot,\cdot)$ is the cosine similarity and $\sigma$ is a fixed scaling
295	constant, with $K_{0}\!=\!1$ at the anchor, which carries a single out vector, and
296	 $K_{s}\!=\!K$ at every speculative slot. Figure 1(b) shows the lattice and the pair of vectors each

299	coupled by a score, yet the vectors that form that score depend on the entire lattice, so a pair at
300	slots $s$ and $s\!+\!1$ may be judged compatible on evidence lying outside them, among the
301	candidates that precede $s$ or follow $s\!+\!1$ . We hypothesize that this is the more useful place
302	to spend capacity: rather than enrich the coupling itself, we keep it pairwise and let the vectors
303	it multiplies see the whole block. The pairwise form is what leaves the scores computable as
304	batched matrix products.
305	Casting each score as a cosine is a deliberate stabilizer: it removes vector magnitude as an

330	recover it. The second follows from prefix acceptance. We condition each transition on the
331	ground-truth predecessor $g_{s-1}$ : a path that has already left the ground truth is discarded by

342	concentrates on earlier slots.

344	The per-slot cross-entropy raises the ground-truth probability but is indifferent to how the
345	residual mass is distributed among the remaining candidates. Under cross-entropy supervision

507	5 Conclusion
508	LiLiCorr correlates the per-slot marginals of a parallel block drafter in a single network
509	pass. Assigning each candidate an in and an out vector reduces the correlation to
510	batched matrix products, leaving only a greedy walk that touches no network weights. Trained
511	jointly with the drafter, LiLiCorr improves on the vanilla DFlash drafter on every benchmark we
512	test, and a draft of comparable quality at a fraction of the cost of correcting one slot at a time
513	makes it the faster system almost everywhere we measure.
514	One limitation is inherent to the design: LiLiCorr reranks only the top- $K$ tokens the
515	drafter proposes, so a slot whose correct token is absent from that pool cannot be recovered, and
516	the achievable acceptance length is bounded by the drafter’s coverage. A second follows from scoring the block
517	through adjacent pairs alone. Each candidate is represented from the whole block, so evidence from
518	distant slots reaches a pair score, but only after being compressed into that one number. Coupling
519	distant slots explicitly is a natural next step, and whether it repays its cost remains open.

forward pass: parallel and diffusion-style block heads such as DFlash (Chen et al., 2026) and diffusion-based self-speculation (Fu et al., 2026) handle a long
speculative window cheaply. D-PACE (Wu et al., 2026) improves DFlash with an
acceptance-aware training objective. Their parallel
prediction mirrors that of diffusion language models, such as LLaDA
(Nie et al., 2026), MDLM (Sahoo et al., 2024), Dream (Ye et al., 2025), and
Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion (Fu et al., 2026). These models exhibit a well-known marginals
limitation: although attention is bidirectional, the block is factorized into
independent per-position predictions, so the sampled tokens are not guaranteed to be
jointly coherent. This is addressed via an iterative refinement, re-masking and re-predicting
subsets of tokens so that later rounds condition on earlier ones. Parallel drafters
inherit the same limitation, but in speculative decoding each refinement round adds a
full drafter pass, which negates the latency gains that motivate parallel drafting. Recovering
coherence without repeated drafter passes is the problem LiLiCorr addresses.
Recovering coherent drafts.
Several recent methods recover a coherent
sequence from the per-slot marginals that a parallel drafter such as DFlash produces.
One direction expands these
marginals into a draft tree of several continuations that the target verifies in a
single pass. DDTree (Ringel and Romano, 2026) is training-free, ranking candidate prefixes by
their marginal product, whereas Oda et al. (2026) first learn a small autoregressive
adapter before building the tree. Both push the correlation work onto the target,
spending the compute speculative decoding aims to save, and both rely on
tree-structured attention, which is typically less efficient than standard causal
attention. An alternative direction reintroduces the dependencies at draft time: Domino
(Huang et al., 2026) and DSpark (Cheng et al., 2026), two of the works developed concurrently with ours,
condition each slot on the previously
sampled tokens, which avoids extra target passes but runs a correction network once at
every slot.
A third work developed concurrently with ours, DFlash2 (Inco AI, 2026), correlates the
block without such a per-slot pass. It learns two embedding tables over the vocabulary, one holding
a vector for each token as a predecessor and one for each token as a successor, and scores a pair of
neighboring tokens by the inner product of the two. The score is added to the drafter’s logits, and
the block is filled left to right, each slot committing the candidate that scores best against the
token just committed. What a pair receives is therefore fixed by the identities of its two tokens,
the same score in every draft. DFlash2 introduces a second and independent contribution, a grouped
causal convolution inside each draft layer that lets neighboring slots exchange local information
while the block stays parallel. The convolution acts on the drafter rather than on the correlation,
so the two compose, and we ablate it on top of LiLiCorr in Appendix C.
The marginals problem is not unique to speculative decoding: non-autoregressive translation
meets it in the same form, and Sun et al. (2019) correlate a parallel decoder by factorizing
adjacent-pair scores into per-token vectors over a top- $K$ pool. What differs here is that
speculative decoding credits only an accepted prefix, which is why LiLiCorr normalizes each slot
locally and commits greedily rather than decoding the best-scoring path.
LiLiCorr also acts at draft time and in a single pass: it produces
all candidate representations at once, computes their pairwise correlations in
parallel, and leaves only a cheap greedy argmax over the resulting scores to run
sequentially. Its vectors are formed from every candidate in the block, so the score of a pair
reflects the context of the entire draft rather than the two token identities alone.
3 Method
3.1 Setup: prefix acceptance and the marginal drafter
Let $M$ be a frozen target language model. A parallel block drafter proposes, in a
single forward pass, a block of $B$ positions conditioned on the verified
context, of which $B-1$ are future tokens. The first block position is the last token
the target has committed, which serves as the anchor, slot $0$ . The remaining $B-1$ positions are
the speculative slots $1,\dots,B-1$ . At each slot the drafter produces a distribution (logit) over the
vocabulary, a per-slot marginal. Standard decoding resolves each slot
independently, taking its most probable token. Once the draft is complete, the
target verifies the whole block in a single pass and accepts a prefix of it,
discarding everything from the first rejected position onward. With a greedy target a draft
token is accepted when it coincides with the target’s own choice. Under a sampling target,
acceptance instead follows the standard rejection test, which preserves the target distribution
exactly (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). In both regimes acceptance is
prefix-structured, and it is this structure that LiLiCorr is built around.
3.2 A scoring model over the candidate lattice
The drafter is supervised on per-slot marginals, so the tokens it selects are
individually probable but not necessarily compatible with one another. Selecting tokens
that are jointly compatible, and not only locally probable, can lengthen the accepted
prefix, and doing so at draft time could avoid extra target passes.
LiLiCorr addresses this goal by correlating the slots over a small pool of alternatives that the
drafter’s own marginal already places near the top. At each slot $s$ it retains the drafter’s
top- $K$ candidate tokens $c_{s,1},\dots,c_{s,K}$ rather than its single most probable
one. Each candidate is a token, and we represent it by a vector we call its node,
formed by summing four terms of equal width: the target’s frozen input embedding of the token, the
drafter’s hidden state at that slot, a small network over a few scalar features of how confident
the drafter is in that candidate, listed in Appendix A, and learned encodings of the
slot and of the candidate’s rank. The hidden state belongs to the slot and is shared by its $K$ 
candidates, so what separates them is the token itself, its confidence, and its rank. Across the
 $B-1$ slots these nodes form a $(B\!-\!1)\times K$ lattice.
A small Transformer processes the $(B\!-\!1)\times K$ nodes jointly. Its self-attention
lets every candidate exchange information with every other, both the competing candidates
within a slot and the candidates at neighboring slots, so each is represented in
the context of the whole block rather than on its own. Each attended node is then fused with a projection of the target’s hidden state that produced
the last verified token: the candidate’s own state, that projection, and their elementwise product
are concatenated and mapped back to the node width by a single layer. Though one vector common to
the whole block, it enters every candidate separately, so that the verifier’s view of the context,
and not the drafter’s alone, shapes each of them.
For each node LiLiCorr emits two
vectors in $\mathbb{R}^{d_{e}}$ , an out vector $\mathbf{o}$ and an in vector $\mathbf{i}$ , each
normalized to unit norm. The dimension $d_{e}$ is given in Appendix A. The anchor,
which precedes the first slot, is encoded far more thinly: the anchor projection itself, mapped by
its own head to one further out vector. Indexing the anchor as slot $0$ , we
write this vector $\mathbf{o}_{0}$ .
Adjacent slots $s$ and $s+1$ are then coupled by a single matching term, the cosine
similarity between the out and in vectors: | |$\phi^{\mathrm{p}}(s,k,k^{\prime})=\sigma\,\cossim(\mathbf{o}_{s,k},\,\mathbf{i}_{s+1,k^{\prime}})~~~~\mbox{for}~~~s=0,\dots,B-2,~~~1\leq k\leq K_{s},~1\leq k^{\prime}\leq K,$  | |(1)
where $\cossim(\cdot,\cdot)$ is the cosine similarity and $\sigma$ is a fixed scaling
constant, with $K_{0}\!=\!1$ at the anchor, which carries a single out vector, and
 $K_{s}\!=\!K$ at every speculative slot. Figure 1(b) shows the lattice and the pair of vectors each
candidate carries.
The factorization is local, but the information behind it is not. Only adjacent slots are
coupled by a score, yet the vectors that form that score depend on the entire lattice, so a pair at
slots $s$ and $s\!+\!1$ may be judged compatible on evidence lying outside them, among the
candidates that precede $s$ or follow $s\!+\!1$ . We hypothesize that this is the more useful place
to spend capacity: rather than enrich the coupling itself, we keep it pairwise and let the vectors
it multiplies see the whole block. The pairwise form is what leaves the scores computable as
batched matrix products.
Casting each score as a cosine is a deliberate stabilizer: it removes vector magnitude as an
unconstrained degree of freedom. Without this bound we observe runaway score magnitudes that
corrupt, and in practice destroy, the shared DFlash backbone under joint training. The cosine
instead confines every learned factor to $[-\sigma,\sigma]$ while avoiding saturating
nonlinearities whose gradients vanish. We use a fixed scale $\sigma$ to separate the candidate scores to discriminate
among them. Its value, and the architecture of the head, are given in Appendix A.
3.3 Training the reranker
Local normalization aligned with prefix acceptance.
A natural formulation scores each full path by summing its matching terms across the block
and selects the path that maximizes this whole-chain score. We argue that this is the wrong target
under prefix acceptance. The global optimum may sacrifice an early slot to win a richer tail, yet
under prefix acceptance that tail is never reached. Section 3.5 and
Appendix F take up this comparison at decoding time. Optimizing the whole
chain thus spends capacity on regions the metric never credits. We therefore score each slot locally,
conditioned on the candidate committed just before it. Writing the per-slot
node score of candidate $k$ as $z_{s}[k]$ , the chain rule factorizes the path distribution
as | |$P_{\theta}(c_{s}\mid c_{s-1})=\softmax_{k}\big(z_{s}[k]\big),\qquad z_{s}[k]=\phi^{\mathrm{p}}(s\!-\!1,\,c_{s-1},\,k),\qquad s=1,\dots,B-1,$  | |(2)
where $c_{s}$ is the candidate committed at slot $s$ and $c_{0}$ is the anchor.
Each conditional still depends on the previous pick through the matching term in $z_{s}[k]$ , so
locality avoids scoring the whole chain without reducing the model to a per-slot reranker.
Oracle-prefix supervision.
We train LiLiCorr as a teacher-forced reranker over
the drafter’s marginals, so the supervision must reflect how it is served. Two conditions
decide which slots carry a learning signal. The first is coverage: a slot is useful only when its
ground-truth token is among the drafter’s $K$ candidates, since otherwise no reranking can
recover it. The second follows from prefix acceptance. We condition each transition on the
ground-truth predecessor $g_{s-1}$ : a path that has already left the ground truth is discarded by
the verifier, so the transitions leaving it are never exercised in serving. A slot is therefore
supervised only when every earlier slot is covered as well. Together these define the
oracle prefix, the longest leading run of slots that each contain the ground-truth token
among their $K$ candidates. Let $\mathcal{S}$ collect these slots across a training batch. We
teacher-force the per-slot cross-entropy on them: | |$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}\;=\;-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\!\!\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\log P_{\theta}\big(c_{s}=g_{s}\mid c_{s-1}=g_{s-1}\big),$  | |(3)
where $g_{s}$ is the ground-truth token at slot $s$ . The softmax of Eq. (2) runs
over all $K$ candidates at slot $s$ , so each supervised transition raises the ground-truth
successor and pushes its $K\!-\!1$ competitors down. A block whose very first slot already
misses contributes zero loss. The effect resembles the per-slot decay used to train DFlash,
though it arises from the coverage mask rather than from a designed weighting: supervision
concentrates on earlier slots.
Target-weighted distractor penalty.
The per-slot cross-entropy raises the ground-truth probability but is indifferent to how the
residual mass is distributed among the remaining candidates. Under cross-entropy supervision
alone, we observed that LiLiCorr’s errors were typically candidates the target scored well-below the ground truth, a mismatch with the verifier rather than a genuine ambiguity in the
target distribution. Since the target is itself the verifier, its logits provide a graded measure
of candidate compatibility that cross-entropy ignores. Scoring against the target lets us direct
the negative gradient at these high-scoring but target-incompatible competitors, widening the
ground truth’s margin over the candidates most likely to trigger an early verification failure.
Let $q_{k}$ denote the target probability of candidate $k$ , and $g_{s}$ the ground-truth candidate at
slot $s$ . Both $q_{g_{s}}$ and the $q_{k}$ are indexed out of the teacher-forced target pass that
already supplies the drafter’s supervision. We define | |$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dist}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}\Omega_{s},\qquad\Omega_{s}=\sum_{k}P_{\theta}\!\left(c_{s}=k\mid c_{s-1}=g_{s-1}\right)\relu\!\left(\log q_{g_{s}}-\log q_{k}\right),$  | |(4)
where $\Omega_{s}$ is the target-relative cost LiLiCorr expects to pay at slot $s$ under its own
distribution, which are averaged over the supervised slots in $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dist}}$ .
Candidates the target ranks below $g_{s}$ are
penalized in proportion to the gap, and those it ranks above are not penalized at all. When $g_{s}$ 
is the target’s top candidate, this
term shares its gradient with a target cross-entropy over the candidate pool, and the rectifier
extends it safely to the rare positions where $g_{s}$ is not the target’s top candidate, as
detailed in Appendix E.
We keep it alongside the
hard cross-entropy because the two supply complementary gradients. Cross-entropy makes LiLiCorr rank the ground truth first even when the target assigns it only modest probability, so it
remains the selected token however soft the target is. The distractor penalty complements this by pushing
the confusers the target disfavors further down. It is therefore cost-aware shaping of
cross-entropy, not a replacement, as detailed in Appendix E.
3.4 Co-adapting the drafter and the reranker
We tune DFlash jointly with LiLiCorr, so that the drafter learns to expose candidate
pools and hidden representations from which LiLiCorr can assemble longer accepted prefixes.
Joint training must cross the top- $K$ selection that forms the candidate pool, which is
not differentiable. We keep the selected candidate indices fixed and retain gradients through their
draft log-probabilities and the hidden states from which they were produced,11
 1
 The
candidate token embeddings remain frozen. both of which are inputs to LiLiCorr. The
acceptance-oriented loss therefore reaches the DFlash backbone without differentiating pool
membership, and inference is unchanged.
The drafter keeps its own DFlash training loss, a per-slot block cross-entropy over the drafter
marginals that weights earlier slots more heavily (Chen et al., 2026), | |$\mathcal{L}_{\text{DFlash }}=-\sum_{s=1}^{B-1}w_{s}\,\log p_{s}(g_{s}),\qquad w_{s}=\exp\!\left(-\frac{s-1}{\beta}\right),$  | |(5)
where $p_{s}$ is the drafter’s marginal at slot $s$ and $\beta$ sets the decay. The drafter and
LiLiCorr are trained jointly to minimize the drafter loss together with the two reranker terms, | |$\mathcal{L}\;=\;\mathcal{L}_{\text{DFlash }}\;+\;\gamma\left[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}\;+\;\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dist}}\right].$  | |(6)
Here $\gamma$ sets the weight of the reranker objective as a whole and $\lambda$ scales the
distractor penalty within it. These weights and the decay $\beta$ are given in
Appendix A. Appendix D ablates the distractor penalty at a fixed
objective weight: it raises acceptance length on all nine benchmarks, and by $1.5\%$ on the
average.
3.5 Single-pass decoding
Decoding has a parallel- and a sequential stage, and the network runs only
once. In the parallel stage, a single LiLiCorr pass produces every outgoing and incoming
vector, including the anchor out vector. The block has $B-1$ adjacent slot pairs, and within
each pair every candidate is matched against every candidate in the next slot. This gives
 $K^{2}$ comparisons for each of the $B\!-\!2$ interior pairs and $K$ for the anchor pair,
 $(B\!-\!2)K^{2}+K$ matching terms in total. Evaluating
them reduces to one matrix multiplication per slot pair, batched across the full block, which
keeps the computation static in shape and well suited to kernel fusion and graph capture. In the sequential stage, the block is committed greedily from left to
right: at slot $s$ we select | |$\hat{c}_{s}\;=\;\argmax_{k}\,z_{s}[k]\;=\;\argmax_{k}\,\phi^{\mathrm{p}}(s\!-\!1,\,\hat{c}_{s-1},\,k),$  | |(7)
conditioning each slot on the candidate just committed, a walk traced in
Figure 1(c). This greedy rule is exactly
the inference behavior the local objective in Eq. (2) was trained
to optimize. An alternative is to commit the path that maximizes the sum of the matching terms.
Appendix F recovers that path exactly with a dynamic program and finds it decodes
worse than the greedy rule. Only the argmax walk is sequential, and it touches no network
weights; the expensive computation is the single parallel pass. This is the key
distinction from iterative-refinement drafters, which invoke a network once per
position: LiLiCorr confines all learning to one pass and reduces the
per-position work to an argmax over precomputed matching scores.
4 Experiments
4.1 Experimental setup
Models and evaluation.
We use frozen Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B targets
(Yang et al., 2025) with their reasoning mode disabled. Evaluation spans eight public datasets across three domains: math (GSM8K,
MATH-500, AIME 2025), code (HumanEval, MBPP, LiveCodeBench), and chat (Alpaca, MT-Bench).
We additionally report on SPEED-Bench (Abramovich et al., 2026), hereafter SPEED, whose
qualitative split holds 880 prompts across eleven categories. We evaluate two decoding regimes: a
deterministic one with a greedy target, and a sampling one at temperature $1$ over the untruncated
target distribution, verified by exact rejection sampling so that the target distribution is
preserved and averaged over three seeds. We measure the acceptance length $\tau$ , computed
block-weighted as the total number of accepted tokens divided by the number of verification
blocks, together with output throughput and the resulting speedup over the target’s own autoregressive
decoding on the same hardware. Three ablations are deferred to
Appendices D, F and C: the distractor penalty, the
greedy decode rule, and DFlash2’s convolution placed in the DFlash backbone that precedes
LiLiCorr.
Baselines.
We compare LiLiCorr against three concurrent works to ours, Domino Huang et al. (2026),
DSpark Cheng et al. (2026) and DFlash2 Inco AI (2026), and against the DFlash drafter it builds on.
All three tune the DFlash drafter as they train their own head, as LiLiCorr does. DFlash2’s convolution acts on the drafter
rather than on the correlation head, so the two compose, and we ablate it on top of LiLiCorr in
Appendix C. At temperature $1$ 
the verifier’s rejection-sampling step reproduces the target distribution however the block was
drafted, so a drafter is free either to commit each slot to its own argmax or to sample its
proposal. Domino and DFlash only take the argmax, whereas LiLiCorr, DSpark and
DFlash2 do both. Table 1 reports the sampled proposal where a system has
one and the argmax otherwise, and Table 7 reports every system under the
argmax. All systems are trained
on the same corpus, for the same number of epochs and at the same global
batch size and sequence length, under an identical configuration across systems and target
sizes, so acceptance length and throughput are directly comparable.

Implementation details.
We serve every system on the same deployment-representative
SGLang backend, with block size 16 on a single H100 and concurrency one
unless stated otherwise. Every speculative head is folded into the drafter and optimized with
fused kernels and graph capture. Fully
optimized, the LiLiCorr head costs $0.299$ ms per
block, against Domino’s $0.611$ and DSpark’s $0.779$ , and accounts for about $3\%$ of the per-block
wall on Qwen3-8B and $4.5\%$ on the cheaper Qwen3-4B block (Figure 2).
DFlash2’s head and convolution together are slightly cheaper, at $0.256$ ms. Table 3
presents these as shares of the block, and the per-stage
decomposition behind them is in Appendix A.
Acceptance length is reproducible to the digits we print, but throughput is not: repeated runs
of one system on one node at concurrency one differ by up to $0.94\%$ . We therefore set the noise
floor at $1\%$ , reading a throughput difference of at most that as a tie and counting a win only
where a system leads every other by more.
Training data.
All systems are trained on roughly $1.4$ M examples
drawn from the code, mathematics, STEM, and general-chat splits of the Nemotron Post-Training
Dataset V2 (Nathawani et al., 2025), with the multilingual splits excluded and every assistant turn
regenerated with the target model (Appendix A).

within that length.

5 Conclusion
LiLiCorr correlates the per-slot marginals of a parallel block drafter in a single network
pass. Assigning each candidate an in and an out vector reduces the correlation to
batched matrix products, leaving only a greedy walk that touches no network weights. Trained
jointly with the drafter, LiLiCorr improves on the vanilla DFlash drafter on every benchmark we
test, and a draft of comparable quality at a fraction of the cost of correcting one slot at a time
makes it the faster system almost everywhere we measure.
One limitation is inherent to the design: LiLiCorr reranks only the top- $K$ tokens the
drafter proposes, so a slot whose correct token is absent from that pool cannot be recovered, and
the achievable acceptance length is bounded by the drafter’s coverage. A second follows from scoring the block
through adjacent pairs alone. Each candidate is represented from the whole block, so evidence from
distant slots reaches a pair score, but only after being compressed into that one number. Coupling
distant slots explicitly is a natural next step, and whether it repays its cost remains open.

Appendix A Implementation and Training Details
Architecture.
Each candidate enters the head as one vector of the head’s hidden width, formed by summing
four terms. The first is the target’s input embedding of the candidate token, held frozen and
projected down. The second is the drafter’s hidden state at that slot, projected down and shared by
the slot’s $K$ candidates. The third is a two-layer network over five scalars describing the
drafter’s confidence in the candidate, all read from its distribution at that slot: the
log-probability and the probability under the full vocabulary, the log-probability gap to the
slot’s most likely token, the rank normalized to $[0,1]$ , and an indicator for being the slot’s top

546	Candidate pool size.
547	We fixed $K$ at $8$ after trying smaller and larger
548	pools. At $K\!=\!4$ fewer slots contain the ground-truth token, so the reranker has less to

556	Objective.
557	The DFlash cross-entropy of Eq. (5) is applied at every slot, whereas the
558	LiLiCorr terms are evaluated only on the oracle prefix, the maximal run of leading slots in which
559	the ground-truth token is present in the candidate pool. Slots beyond the first coverage miss

663	Appendix C The Convolution Variant
664	DFlash2 contributes a grouped causal convolution inside the draft layers alongside its
665	candidate selector. The two are independent: the convolution improves the drafter, and is
666	indifferent to how the candidates it proposes are afterwards correlated. We therefore place it
667	under LiLiCorr as well and report the resulting arm, LiLiCorr + conv, here rather than in the main tables,
668	since the question it answers is not how LiLiCorr compares with the baselines but how much a better
669	drafter adds on top of it.
670	Table 12 gives the nine benchmarks at both target sizes and both decoding
671	regimes. Its baseline columns are the same measurement as in Table 1, so the
672	two tables may be read against one another. Table 13 isolates what the convolution
673	itself buys. Under greedy decoding it raises acceptance length over LiLiCorr by $2.3\%$ on Qwen3-8B
674	and $2.5\%$ on Qwen3-4B on the nine-benchmark average, and on every one of the eighteen benchmarks
675	individually. It converts that into throughput at the
676	larger target size, by $0.6\%$ on the average, but not at the smaller, where its fixed per-block
677	cost is a larger share of a cheaper block. Over the seventy-two settings of
678	Section 4.2 the arm holds the highest throughput at $64$ , ties at $6$ and trails at
679	 $2$ , against $63$ , $6$ and $3$ for LiLiCorr, and it removes both HumanEval deficits: at Qwen3-4B it
680	accepts $5.4\%$ more than DFlash2 where LiLiCorr accepts $3.0\%$ less. On the concurrency sweep of
681	Section 4.3 it leads all thirty-six operating points, as LiLiCorr does, with an
682	acceptance margin over the strongest baseline in each cell of $2.2$ to $10.4\%$ against LiLiCorr’s
683	 $1.1$ to $5.7\%$ . Table 14 places the two side by side there: the convolution
684	accepts more at every one of the thirty-six points, by $0.3$ to $5.2\%$ , and serves faster at
685	twenty-six of them. The convolution is not free: it adds $0.136$ ms per block, raising the cost of the

713	Appendix E Derivations for the Reranker Objective
714	The distractor penalty is an expected target cost.
715	Write $P_{\theta}(k)$ for $P_{\theta}(c_{s}=k\mid c_{s-1}=g_{s-1})$ , let $c_{k}=-\log q_{k}$ be the
716	cost the target assigns to candidate $k$ , low where the target is confident, and let
717	 $w_{k}=\relu(c_{k}-c_{g_{s}})$ be that cost relative to the ground truth after rectification. The penalty
718	of Eq. (4) is then $\Omega_{s}=\sum_{k}P_{\theta}(k)\,w_{k}$ , the expected rectified cost
719	of the candidate LiLiCorr commits to. When $g_{s}$ is the target’s preferred candidate in the pool no
720	cost is negative, the rectifier is inactive, and since $\sum_{k}P_{\theta}(k)=1$ , | |$\Omega_{s}\;=\;\sum_{k}P_{\theta}(k)\,\left(c_{k}-c_{g_{s}}\right)\;=\;H(P_{\theta},q)-c_{g_{s}},\qquad H(P_{\theta},q)=\sum_{k}P_{\theta}(k)\,c_{k}.$  | |(8)
721	 $H(P_{\theta},q)$ is the expected target cost under $P_{\theta}$ , and the offset $c_{g_{s}}$ does not
722	depend on the LiLiCorr parameters, so $\nabla_{\theta}\Omega_{s}=\nabla_{\theta}H(P_{\theta},q)$ : the
723	penalty and a cross-entropy against the target have the same gradient. The penalty involves the
724	target only through cost differences, so it is unchanged if $q$ is renormalized over the pool.
725	Why this is not distribution matching.
726	The target is frozen, so the costs $c_{k}$ are constants and $\Omega_{s}$ is linear in $P_{\theta}$ .
727	A linear function on the probability simplex attains its minimum at a vertex, that is, at a
728	distribution placing all of its mass on one candidate, and the minimizing vertex is the candidate
729	of least cost. Under the assumption above that candidate is $g_{s}$ , so minimizing the penalty drives
730	LiLiCorr to commit to the target’s preferred candidate rather than to reproduce the target’s
731	distribution over the pool. Committing is what the verifier rewards, since a block is accepted on
732	the tokens the target would itself emit and mass placed elsewhere is not recovered.
733	The rectifier.
734	At the occasional slot where $g_{s}$ is not the target’s preferred candidate, the rectifier
735	clips the negative costs that would otherwise reward a candidate the target ranks above the
736	supervised token. Such slots are rare, and arise from numerical differences between the offline
737	generation of the supervision and the teacher-forced target pass used during training, rather than
738	from a genuine target preference.
739	Complementary gradients.
740	The hard cross-entropy and the distractor penalty act on the ground-truth logit $z_{g}$ through
741	complementary gradients. For cross-entropy, | |$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial z_{g}}=P_{\theta}(g)-1,$  | |(9)
742	which remains strong when $P_{\theta}(g)$ is small, exactly the hardest mistakes. For the penalty, | |$\frac{\partial\Omega_{s}}{\partial z_{g}}=-\,P_{\theta}(g)\,\mathbb{E}_{P_{\theta}}[w],$  | |(10)
743	which vanishes as $P_{\theta}(g)\to 0$ , so the penalty alone is weak precisely when the ground
744	truth is badly misranked. It is also indifferent among candidates of zero cost, including target
745	ties and candidates the target ranks above $g$ , since the rectifier clips their costs to zero.
746	Cross-entropy therefore robustly pulls the exact ground-truth token upward, while $\Omega_{s}$ 
747	preferentially pushes target-rejected confusers downward, so the penalty is best viewed as
748	cost-aware shaping of cross-entropy rather than a replacement for it. Both terms are evaluated
749	only on the oracle prefix and averaged over the same slots, so slots after the first coverage miss
750	contribute to neither.
751	Appendix F Greedy Selection Versus the Highest-Scoring Path
752	Sections 3.3 and 3.5 argue that prefix acceptance rewards a
753	greedy left-to-right decode over a search for the best-scoring block. We test the decode rule
754	in isolation, holding the trained model fixed and varying only the rule that selects a path
755	through the candidate lattice.
756	Path selection.
757	Let $c=(c_{1},\dots,c_{B-1})$ denote a path, where $c_{s}$ is the candidate committed at
758	slot $s$ and $c_{0}$ is the anchor. Since LiLiCorr couples only adjacent slots, a path scores as
759	the sum of its matching terms, | |$g(c)\;=\;\sum_{s=1}^{B-1}\phi^{\mathrm{p}}\!\left(s\!-\!1,\,c_{s-1},\,c_{s}\right).$  | |(11)
760	The greedy rule of Section 3.5 commits each slot to the best continuation of
761	what precedes it and never revisits an earlier choice. The alternative is to return the path
762	that maximizes $g$ . Enumeration is infeasible, as the lattice holds
763	 $K^{B-1}$ paths, but the pairwise structure of Eq. (11) makes the
764	exact maximizer reachable in $O(B\,K^{2})$ time by dynamic programming. Sweeping
765	left to right, one records for each candidate the score of the best path ending there,
766	then traces the stored predecessors back from the best final candidate. This is the Viterbi
767	algorithm (Viterbi, 1967), a strictly stronger optimizer of $g$ than the greedy walk.
768	Why the stronger optimizer is not the better one here.
769	Under prefix acceptance every slot contributes only while all the slots before it have
770	matched, so the early ones carry most of the expected acceptance length, and a block that
771	loses its first slot gains nothing from the rest. Maximizing $g$ targets the block as a whole,
772	which is essentially the probability that the entire block survives verification. Giving up an
773	early slot to raise the total is rational for that objective and self-defeating here, because
774	the improved tail is never reached. The greedy walk instead maximizes the leading decision
775	exactly, and each later one conditioned on what was committed.

choice. The fourth is a pair of learned tables, one
indexed by slot and one by rank. The target state that every candidate is later fused with is
formed separately: the target’s hidden states that produced the last verified token, collapsed
across five captured layers, normalized, and projected to the same width.
The head itself is a two-layer bidirectional Transformer over the
 $(B\!-\!1)\times K$ candidate lattice, attending over all of it at once, with hidden width
 $1024$ , eight attention heads, and a feed-forward width of $2048$ , using RMSNorm and SiLU
activations. Beyond the slot table, position enters through two attention biases learned per head
and added to the attention logits, one indexed by the signed slot distance between a pair and one
marking pairs of candidates that occupy the same slot. Only after the Transformer is each candidate
combined with that target state, by concatenating the candidate state, the target state, and their
elementwise product, and projecting the result back down to the head’s width through a single
linear layer followed by a SiLU. This is the one concatenation in the head, everything else being a
sum. Two linear heads then emit the out and in vectors of
Section 3.2, each of dimension $d_{e}$ and normalized to unit norm, and a third emits
the anchor’s single out vector. Table 4 presents the settings.
Candidate pool size.
We fixed $K$ at $8$ after trying smaller and larger
pools. At $K\!=\!4$ fewer slots contain the ground-truth token, so the reranker has less to
recover; at $K\!=\!16$ coverage improves, but the added candidates are ones the drafter already
ranks low and the wider lattice costs more per block. Both served slower than $K\!=\!8$ in our
runs.
Training corpus.
For each conversation we keep the original system and user
messages and regenerate every assistant turn with the target model, decoding greedily with
reasoning disabled and a cap of $4{,}096$ completion tokens.
Objective.
The DFlash cross-entropy of Eq. (5) is applied at every slot, whereas the
LiLiCorr terms are evaluated only on the oracle prefix, the maximal run of leading slots in which
the ground-truth token is present in the candidate pool. Slots beyond the first coverage miss
contribute to none of the three terms.
Serving.
We fuse top- $K$ candidate extraction and vocabulary-wide logit normalization into a single
kernel, compile the matching and selection step, and use wide CUDA graphs that fold candidate
pooling and reranking into a single replay. The same level of optimization is applied to Domino’s
correction loop. Table 3 gives the resulting per-block cost of each head and is
the source of the figures quoted in Section 4.1.
Isolating the head.
Table 3 is obtained by subtraction. Every benchmark run under greedy decoding
reports throughput and
acceptance length, and their ratio is the wall-clock time of one verification block. The DFlash control is the same system with no reranking at all, and its block takes $8.87$ ms on Qwen3-8B and
 $5.88$ ms on Qwen3-4B, so subtracting it from another system’s block time leaves what that system’s
head costs. All six run together in each allocation, so the choice of machine cancels in the
subtraction. We take the median block time over eight of the nine benchmarks, excluding HumanEval,
whose short outputs let prefill dominate, and subtract one median from the other. Two things follow
from measuring a difference rather than a stage. The figure is net of the per-slot argmax the
control performs instead, which is the cost a deployment actually pays for reranking. And it
resolves about $0.03$ ms, the spread across three independent reads of the convolution’s per-block
cost, with per-benchmark head costs varying by up to $\pm 0.1$ ms around the median.

above. For DFlash2 and LiLiCorr + conv the figure covers the drafter-side convolution as well as the
head. | |Qwen3-8B |Qwen3-4B |System |Head (ms) |Share of block |Head (ms) |Share of block |DFlash2 |0.256 |2.8% |0.227 |3.7% |LiLiCorr |0.299 |3.3% |0.276 |4.5% |LiLiCorr + conv |0.436 |4.7% |0.396 |6.3% |Domino |0.611 |6.5% |0.586 |9.1% |DSpark |0.779 |8.1% |0.765 |11.5%
Precision.
The drafter is trained with a full-precision master copy of its weights, and the optimizer moments
are kept in full precision throughout. Two details follow from how that copy is handled. Some
training runs stopped and resumed. On resume the drafter’s weights are reloaded at the target
model’s precision, so the master copy is round-tripped through bf16 at that point, in resumed and
uninterrupted runs alike. Where a resumed run re-covered steps it had already taken, the recomputed
loss values matched the earlier pass to the precision logged. Separately, the drafter is
initialized in full precision, but in the runs reported here that initialization was rounded to the
target’s precision before training began, so that arms differing only in precision started from
numerically identical weights. The rounding moves the initialization only below bf16 resolution and
leaves first-step loss and gradients unchanged.
Baselines.
Domino is served in its widened configuration, trained at $512$ anchors rather than its
released $256$ . Its correction head is a recurrent cell over the drafter’s
hidden width followed by a vocabulary projection. DSpark is served
in a width-matched configuration, and at temperature $1$ under each of
its two proposals, argmax and sampled. Both are run at block size $15$ , so that every arm
drafts the same fifteen tokens and verifies the same sixteen slots. DFlash2 is likewise served under both, and at
its released selector width rather than at ours: matching the two candidate pools would change its
method rather than control a variable, since the two rerankers are different mechanisms at
different budgets, so what we match across arms is the drafted width instead. Each baseline is
composed from its own released branch rather than reimplemented from its published settings, and
DFlash2 specifically is benchmarked through a third-party reimplementation trained under our
contract, since its own sources do not disclose a training recipe. All
systems are trained on the same regenerated corpus for the same six epochs, at the same global
batch size and sequence length, with self-distillation disabled on every arm, and with
drafter and target sharing a rotary base of $10^{6}$ .

Appendix C The Convolution Variant
DFlash2 contributes a grouped causal convolution inside the draft layers alongside its
candidate selector. The two are independent: the convolution improves the drafter, and is
indifferent to how the candidates it proposes are afterwards correlated. We therefore place it
under LiLiCorr as well and report the resulting arm, LiLiCorr + conv, here rather than in the main tables,
since the question it answers is not how LiLiCorr compares with the baselines but how much a better
drafter adds on top of it.
Table 12 gives the nine benchmarks at both target sizes and both decoding
regimes. Its baseline columns are the same measurement as in Table 1, so the
two tables may be read against one another. Table 13 isolates what the convolution
itself buys. Under greedy decoding it raises acceptance length over LiLiCorr by $2.3\%$ on Qwen3-8B
and $2.5\%$ on Qwen3-4B on the nine-benchmark average, and on every one of the eighteen benchmarks
individually. It converts that into throughput at the
larger target size, by $0.6\%$ on the average, but not at the smaller, where its fixed per-block
cost is a larger share of a cheaper block. Over the seventy-two settings of
Section 4.2 the arm holds the highest throughput at $64$ , ties at $6$ and trails at
 $2$ , against $63$ , $6$ and $3$ for LiLiCorr, and it removes both HumanEval deficits: at Qwen3-4B it
accepts $5.4\%$ more than DFlash2 where LiLiCorr accepts $3.0\%$ less. On the concurrency sweep of
Section 4.3 it leads all thirty-six operating points, as LiLiCorr does, with an
acceptance margin over the strongest baseline in each cell of $2.2$ to $10.4\%$ against LiLiCorr’s
 $1.1$ to $5.7\%$ . Table 14 places the two side by side there: the convolution
accepts more at every one of the thirty-six points, by $0.3$ to $5.2\%$ , and serves faster at
twenty-six of them. The convolution is not free: it adds $0.136$ ms per block, raising the cost of the
LiLiCorr head by about half (Table 3).

per-benchmark acceptance lengths at concurrency one. The penalty raises acceptance length on all
nine benchmarks, by $1.5\%$ on the average, most on HumanEval at $3.8\%$ and least on AlpacaEval at
 $0.2\%$ . It is what trains the reranker against the candidates that actually cost acceptances
rather than against the ground-truth label alone, and Appendix E derives it as
an expected target cost.

Appendix E Derivations for the Reranker Objective
The distractor penalty is an expected target cost.
Write $P_{\theta}(k)$ for $P_{\theta}(c_{s}=k\mid c_{s-1}=g_{s-1})$ , let $c_{k}=-\log q_{k}$ be the
cost the target assigns to candidate $k$ , low where the target is confident, and let
 $w_{k}=\relu(c_{k}-c_{g_{s}})$ be that cost relative to the ground truth after rectification. The penalty
of Eq. (4) is then $\Omega_{s}=\sum_{k}P_{\theta}(k)\,w_{k}$ , the expected rectified cost
of the candidate LiLiCorr commits to. When $g_{s}$ is the target’s preferred candidate in the pool no
cost is negative, the rectifier is inactive, and since $\sum_{k}P_{\theta}(k)=1$ , | |$\Omega_{s}\;=\;\sum_{k}P_{\theta}(k)\,\left(c_{k}-c_{g_{s}}\right)\;=\;H(P_{\theta},q)-c_{g_{s}},\qquad H(P_{\theta},q)=\sum_{k}P_{\theta}(k)\,c_{k}.$  | |(8)
 $H(P_{\theta},q)$ is the expected target cost under $P_{\theta}$ , and the offset $c_{g_{s}}$ does not
depend on the LiLiCorr parameters, so $\nabla_{\theta}\Omega_{s}=\nabla_{\theta}H(P_{\theta},q)$ : the
penalty and a cross-entropy against the target have the same gradient. The penalty involves the
target only through cost differences, so it is unchanged if $q$ is renormalized over the pool.
Why this is not distribution matching.
The target is frozen, so the costs $c_{k}$ are constants and $\Omega_{s}$ is linear in $P_{\theta}$ .
A linear function on the probability simplex attains its minimum at a vertex, that is, at a
distribution placing all of its mass on one candidate, and the minimizing vertex is the candidate
of least cost. Under the assumption above that candidate is $g_{s}$ , so minimizing the penalty drives
LiLiCorr to commit to the target’s preferred candidate rather than to reproduce the target’s
distribution over the pool. Committing is what the verifier rewards, since a block is accepted on
the tokens the target would itself emit and mass placed elsewhere is not recovered.
The rectifier.
At the occasional slot where $g_{s}$ is not the target’s preferred candidate, the rectifier
clips the negative costs that would otherwise reward a candidate the target ranks above the
supervised token. Such slots are rare, and arise from numerical differences between the offline
generation of the supervision and the teacher-forced target pass used during training, rather than
from a genuine target preference.
Complementary gradients.
The hard cross-entropy and the distractor penalty act on the ground-truth logit $z_{g}$ through
complementary gradients. For cross-entropy, | |$\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}}{\partial z_{g}}=P_{\theta}(g)-1,$  | |(9)
which remains strong when $P_{\theta}(g)$ is small, exactly the hardest mistakes. For the penalty, | |$\frac{\partial\Omega_{s}}{\partial z_{g}}=-\,P_{\theta}(g)\,\mathbb{E}_{P_{\theta}}[w],$  | |(10)
which vanishes as $P_{\theta}(g)\to 0$ , so the penalty alone is weak precisely when the ground
truth is badly misranked. It is also indifferent among candidates of zero cost, including target
ties and candidates the target ranks above $g$ , since the rectifier clips their costs to zero.
Cross-entropy therefore robustly pulls the exact ground-truth token upward, while $\Omega_{s}$ 
preferentially pushes target-rejected confusers downward, so the penalty is best viewed as
cost-aware shaping of cross-entropy rather than a replacement for it. Both terms are evaluated
only on the oracle prefix and averaged over the same slots, so slots after the first coverage miss
contribute to neither.
Appendix F Greedy Selection Versus the Highest-Scoring Path
Sections 3.3 and 3.5 argue that prefix acceptance rewards a
greedy left-to-right decode over a search for the best-scoring block. We test the decode rule
in isolation, holding the trained model fixed and varying only the rule that selects a path
through the candidate lattice.
Path selection.
Let $c=(c_{1},\dots,c_{B-1})$ denote a path, where $c_{s}$ is the candidate committed at
slot $s$ and $c_{0}$ is the anchor. Since LiLiCorr couples only adjacent slots, a path scores as
the sum of its matching terms, | |$g(c)\;=\;\sum_{s=1}^{B-1}\phi^{\mathrm{p}}\!\left(s\!-\!1,\,c_{s-1},\,c_{s}\right).$  | |(11)
The greedy rule of Section 3.5 commits each slot to the best continuation of
what precedes it and never revisits an earlier choice. The alternative is to return the path
that maximizes $g$ . Enumeration is infeasible, as the lattice holds
 $K^{B-1}$ paths, but the pairwise structure of Eq. (11) makes the
exact maximizer reachable in $O(B\,K^{2})$ time by dynamic programming. Sweeping
left to right, one records for each candidate the score of the best path ending there,
then traces the stored predecessors back from the best final candidate. This is the Viterbi
algorithm (Viterbi, 1967), a strictly stronger optimizer of $g$ than the greedy walk.
Why the stronger optimizer is not the better one here.
Under prefix acceptance every slot contributes only while all the slots before it have
matched, so the early ones carry most of the expected acceptance length, and a block that
loses its first slot gains nothing from the rest. Maximizing $g$ targets the block as a whole,
which is essentially the probability that the entire block survives verification. Giving up an
early slot to raise the total is rational for that objective and self-defeating here, because
the improved tail is never reached. The greedy walk instead maximizes the leading decision
exactly, and each later one conditioned on what was committed.

The comparison is between decode rules for one trained model, not between formulations:
LiLiCorr is trained under the local objective of Eq. (2), so its path score is

this calibration is worth more than the stronger optimizer, at equal serving cost.
The exact optimizer decodes worse. It lowers acceptance
length on all nine benchmarks, by $0.84$ to $4.46\%$ and by $2.64\%$ on average. Throughput follows,
since the two rules are equally cheap to serve: each is a single fused kernel folded into the same

magnitude; every other benchmark lies between $-0.84\%$ and $-3.43\%$ . The smallest effect is on
HumanEval, which is also the smallest split and carries the largest block-rate excursion of the
nine.
