content.content:
1	Abstract
2	Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) by drafting multiple tokens and verifying them in parallel, but it faces a scaling limitation: increasing the draft budget improves speed only when acceptance remains high and drafting overhead stays low. This ceiling has been difficult to break because prior head-based SD methods face a causality-efficiency dilemma. Autoregressive drafters produce path-conditioned candidates that are effective for tree speculative decoding with higher acceptance length, but their drafting cost grows with tree depth. Bidirectional block-diffusion drafters generate all positions in one pass, but their branch-agnostic marginals can form individually plausible yet mutually inconsistent trees, wasting budget and reducing acceptance. We propose JetSpec, a head-based SD framework that combines one-forward drafting efficiency with causal information flow across draft representations. JetSpec trains a causal parallel draft head using fused hidden states from the frozen target model, producing causally coupled draft distributions whose scores better align with the target model’s autoregressive factorization. This enables JetSpec to convert larger draft budgets into longer accepted prefixes and higher end-to-end speedup. Across math, coding, and chat benchmarks on dense and MoE Qwen3 models, JetSpec consistently outperforms bidirectional-head and tree-based SD baselines. On H100 GPUs, JetSpec achieves up to $9.64\times$ speedup on MATH-500 and $4.58\times$ on open-ended conversational workloads, with further latency gains demonstrated through vLLM integration under realistic serving loads. Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/JetSpec. |
3	1 Introduction
4	Modern autoregressive (AR) Large Language Models (LLMs) operate under a simple yet costly bottleneck: decoding remains largely serial. This sequential generation process makes latency a major challenge when they are deployed in applications such as math (Wei et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2025), coding (Deng et al., 2025; Jain et al., 2024) and other agentic reasoning tasks (Patil et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025), where models often perform long generations.
5	Existing approaches address this challenge by either incorporating multi-token prediction (MTP) during pre-training or mid-training (Gloeckle et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2026; AI, 2026; Xiaomi, 2026), or post-training methods that adapt pretrained LLMs into diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) at the costs of varying degrees of performance degradation (Zhao et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). In contrast, applying speculative decoding (SD) at inference time to reduce generation latency while preserving quality (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023).
6	Among these techniques, SD stands out for its low adaptation cost and simplicity. On one hand, prior work shows that SD performance can be substantially improved through lightweight draft-model alignment, oftentimes less than 1B training tokens (Liu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Goel et al., 2024). On the other hand, head-based methods such as Medusa and EAGLE reduce deployment complexity by avoiding the conventional separate draft-target model setup (Cai et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b). More recent head-based methods such as EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025) and DFlash (Chen et al., 2026) continue to improve drafting quality and reducing drafting cost for better end-to-end acceleration. Despite these advances, head-based SD still faces a causality-efficiency dilemma. Autoregressive drafters such as EAGLE produce high-quality path-conditioned candidates but require sequential draft passes as tree depth grows. Bidirectional block-diffusion drafters such as DFlash produces drafts in one pass, but their branch-agnostic marginals can form individually plausible yet mutually inconsistent trees, wasting budget and reducing acceptance.
7	We propose JetSpec, a SD framework designed to break this causality–efficiency dilemma: JetSpec trains a causal parallel draft head to predict distributions for multiple draft depths in one forward pass while enforcing left-to-right information flow across draft-position hidden states. This produces causal depth-wise marginals that better reflect autoregressive continuation structure, enabling tree acceptance to scale more effectively with draft budget.
8	Empirically, JetSpec demonstrates significant efficiency gains. In the low-token-budget regime with 16 draft tokens, JetSpec achieves competitive end-to-end speedup.
9	In the high-token-budget regime with 256 draft tokens, JetSpec achieves strong gains, reaching $\tau=10.7$ and $9.5\times$ speedup on MATH-500, and remaining effective on MT-Bench with $\tau=5.9$ and over $4\times$ speedup. We further integrate JetSpec into industry-grade serving engine and evaluate it across batch sizes, where it consistently outperforms baselines under small to moderate serving loads, with especially strong gains on higher-end GPUs such as H100 and B200. These results highlight the practical potential of JetSpec for reducing decoding latency in serving.
10	Figure 1: 
11	End-to-end decoding speedup over standard autoregressive decoding on H100 GPUs across math, coding, and chat benchmarks. DFlash denotes the original block-parallel drafting method, DDTree is tree-based variant of DFlash, and JetSpec denotes our method. Both employ a tree budget of 256 tokens using Algorithm 1.
12	In a nutshell, our work makes the following contributions:
13	• 
14	We propose JetSpec, a paradigm designed to jointly optimize drafting cost and acceptance rate for speculative decoding. JetSpec trains a causal prediction head with parallel tree-drafting capability, enabling low-cost draft generation while preserving causal dependencies across draft-depth representations.
15	• 
16	We develop and evaluate tree-drafting algorithms that allow speculative decoding to better leverage additional decoding compute. By scaling the draft token budget, JetSpec achieves up to $\tau=10.7$ and more than $9.5\times$ end-to-end speedup.
17	• 
18	We integrate JetSpec into an industry-grade serving engine and evaluate it under realistic serving scenarios. JetSpec consistently outperforms baselines under small to moderate serving loads, highlighting its practical potential for reducing latency in real-world deployments.
19	2 Related Work
20	Speculative Decoding.
21	Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting tokens and verifying them with the target model (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). Its speedup depends on acceptance length and drafting cost. Prior work improves these factors via draft-target alignment (Zhou et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Goel et al., 2024), head-based drafters such as Medusa (Cai et al., 2024) and EAGLE (Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2025), or draft-free retrieval methods such as Prompt Lookup Decoding (Saxena, 2023), REST (He et al., 2024), PLD+ (Somasundaram et al., 2024), SAM Decoding (Hu et al., 2025b), and SuffixDecoding (Oliaro et al., 2024). While these methods reduce overhead, they often rely on semantic overlaps for retrieval, or repeated patterns. In contrast, JetSpec targets low-cost parallel drafting with a learned causal head that preserves branch-wise dependencies for high-acceptance tree verification.
22	Drafter Alignment.
23	Previous works train draft models or draft heads to better match the target model. Multi-token prediction objectives supervise future-token predictions during pretraining or midtraining (Gloeckle et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024), while post-training approaches use supervised fine-tuning, offline distillation, online distillation, or direct acceptance-rate optimization to improve agreement between draft and target distributions (Zhou et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Goel et al., 2024). These methods primarily improve the alignment term that controls acceptance rate. JetSpec is complementary: it trains the drafter not only to match the target model, but also to preserve directional structure for budgeted tree construction, so tree expansion uses causally coupled draft distributions rather than independent position marginals.
24	Parallel Decoding and Drafting.
25	Parallel decoding methods reduce latency by relaxing strict one-token-at-a-time generation. Self-speculative decoding drafts with early target-model layers and verifies with later layers (Elhoushi et al., 2024). Diffusion LLMs refine multiple tokens per iteration (Wu et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2026). Jacobi-style methods preserve causality by parallel fixed-point updates, with recent consistency distillation works improving convergence to autoregressive outputs (Fu et al., 2024; Kou et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025a). These methods increase tokens committed per forward, but are typically applied to the target model itself. DFlash generates multiple draft tokens in one block-parallel pass (Chen et al., 2026); DDTree further constructs trees from its bidirectional per-position distributions (Ringel and Romano, 2026), while Domino adds a lightweight sequential causal-correction head on top of a parallel drafter to condition later predictions on sampled earlier tokens (Huang et al., 2026); see Appendix B for a detailed comparison. In contrast, JetSpec introduces causal information flow directly within the parallel draft head, producing causally coupled depth-wise distributions for tree construction in a single forward pass.
26	3 JetSpec
27	3.1 Background
28	Scaling Bottlenecks in Speculative Decoding.
29	In speculative decoding (SD), a lightweight draft model $M_{q}$ proposes $N$ tokens, which are verified in parallel by the target model $M_{p}$  (Leviathan et al., 2023). The target accepts the longest prefix consistent with its predictions and resumes from the first rejected token. Let $\alpha$ denote the average acceptance rate and $c$ the per-step cost of $M_{q}$ relative to $M_{p}$ . Under the standard i.i.d. acceptance assumption, | |$\mathbb{E}[\#\mathrm{tokens}]=\frac{1-\alpha^{N+1}}{1-\alpha},\qquad\mathrm{Speedup}=\frac{1-\alpha^{N+1}}{(1-\alpha)(Nc+1)}.$  | |(1)
30	Thus, scaling to longer drafts requires both high acceptance $\alpha$ and low total drafting cost $Nc$ : as $N$ grows, even modest acceptance degradation or drafting overhead can offset the gains from parallel verification. Figure 2 illustrates this tradeoff.
31	(a) Typical SD ( $c=0.05$ ).
32	(b) Ultra low-cost SD ( $c=0.0005$ ).
33	Figure 2: 
34	Expected speculative decoding speedup scales as a function of draft length $\gamma$ , under different per-token drafting costs $c$ and acceptance rates $\alpha$ . Comparing the two panels shows that reducing $c$ substantially improves the scalability of speculative decoding with respect to $\gamma$ , and increasing $\alpha$ further amplifies this effect. The results highlight that pushing per-token drafting cost $c$ low and acceptance rate $\alpha$ high is critical for unlocking stronger scaling with longer draft lengths.
35	Existing work usually improves acceptance rate and drafting cost separately. To increase acceptance quality $\alpha$ , draft-model alignment methods improve agreement between $M_{q}$ and $M_{p}$  (Zhou et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Goel et al., 2024), while tree SD methods improve verification efficiency by expanding multiple candidate branches in parallel (Miao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a). To reduce drafting cost $c$ , head-based methods avoid a separately deployed draft model (Cai et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2025); more recently, DFlash further reduces overhead through block-diffusion-style drafting, generating multiple draft tokens in a single draft pass (Chen et al., 2026) (see Appendix G). However, scaling to longer drafts requires simultaneously maintaining high $\alpha$ and low $c$ , motivating JetSpec to jointly improve acceptance rate and drafting efficiency.
36	3.2 Causal Parallel Drafting
37	Can We Realize Both Parallel Drafting and Tree SD?
38	A natural direction to co-optimize both aspects is to combine tree drafting for higher acceptance with parallel drafting for lower cost. However, existing parallel drafting methods such as DFlash can break the causal structure needed for effective tree construction: future-position marginals are produced without causal dependence on earlier draft positions, so high-probability marginals can compose into mutually inconsistent branches. JetSpec addresses this limitation with a causal parallel draft head that couples draft-depth representations left-to-right while preserving the efficiency of one-pass parallel prediction.
39	Why Causality Matters.
40	A tree inherently encodes a causal structure. Consider a draft tree rooted at the original prefix $x$ , where each node $v$ corresponds to a candidate token $y_{v}$ . Let $\pi(v)=(y_{v_{1}},\ldots,y_{v})$ denote the path from the root to $v$ , and $\pi_{<v}$ its ancestor tokens. Ideally, the distribution at each node should reflect its corresponding branch prefix. In contrast, a bidirectional parallel drafter allows each position to attend to representations from both earlier and later draft positions. It creates a mismatch between bidirectional draft representations and the causal structure required for tree construction.
41	Architecture.
42	JetSpec adopts a head-based drafting architecture, where a draft head can reuse intermediate features from the target model. Specifically, DFlash shows that a lightweight block-parallel draft head can reuse target-model hidden states and inject fused target-context features into the draft layers’ KV cache for strong target-model guidance (Chen et al., 2026). Building on this design, JetSpec introduces a causal parallel decoding head for tree drafting.
43	Given a prefix $x$ with fused target-model features $h_{x}^{o}$ , the draft head predicts logits for multiple future positions in parallel. Following standard speculative decoding notation, the target model defines an autoregressive distribution over a length- $k$ continuation: | |$p(y_{1:k}\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}p(y_{i}\mid x,y_{<i}).$  | |(2)
44	To introduce analogous directional dependencies into parallel drafting, we apply a causal attention mask across draft positions. Position $i$ may attend to the prefix features and earlier draft-position hidden states, but not to later positions. The mask and the masked attention at position $i$ are | |$B_{i,j}=\begin{cases}0,&j\leq i,\\
45	-\infty,&j>i,\end{cases},\qquad\mathrm{Attn}(Q_{i},K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{Q_{i}K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}+B_{i}\right)V,$  | |(3)
46	with prefix features visible to all draft positions. This allows all draft positions to be processed in parallel while enforcing directional information flow from earlier to later positions. Consequently, the distribution $r_{i}(\cdot\mid x,h_{x}^{o})$ at position $i$ is computed from a hidden representation that depends causally on earlier draft-position representations, rather than being produced independently across positions.

52	3.3 Training
53	Data Preparation.
54	We train the draft head on target-aligned sequences, obtained either from the training corpus, as in multi-token prediction (Gloeckle et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024), or from
55	continuations regenerated by the target model (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2026). Given a sequence $(x,y_{1:k})$ , we sample anchor positions and, at each anchor, construct a length- $N$ training block of $N$ consecutive future positions. The draft head predicts these $N$ positions in parallel under a block-causal mask, matching the per-position teacher logits produced by the target model on the same ground-truth prefix.
56	Distillation Loss.
57	We train the draft head with a soft-label distillation objective so that the draft distribution preserves the target model’s relative preferences across multiple plausible continuations. Among distillation objectives, forward KL encourages the draft distribution to cover the target model’s probability mass, preserving soft-label information beyond the top prediction. Reverse KL, in contrast, is more mode-seeking and can concentrate probability on high-confidence teacher modes (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024). We find this matters in practice (Section 4): reverse KL underperforms substantially, while forward KL slightly outperforms hard-label SFT. We therefore adopt forward KL by default, and present the loss in this form below.
58	For each active draft position $m$ , let $z_{q}^{(m)}$ and $z_{p}^{(m)}$ denote the draft and target logits over the vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ . We define temperature-normalized distributions
59	 $\tilde{q}^{(m)}=\mathrm{softmax}(z_{q}^{(m)}/T_{\mathrm{KD}})$ 
60	and
61	 $\tilde{p}^{(m)}=\mathrm{softmax}(z_{p}^{(m)}/T_{\mathrm{KD}})$ , and minimize the forward KL | |$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FKL}}^{(m)}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\tilde{p}^{(m)}\,\middle\|\,\tilde{q}^{(m)}\right).$  | |(5)
62	The final objective is computed over all active draft-token positions induced from the training sequence and normalized by the active-position mask (see Appendix D for details): | |$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}=T_{\mathrm{KD}}^{2}\frac{\sum_{m}w_{m}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FKL}}^{(m)}}{\sum_{m}w_{m}},$  | |(6)
63	where $m$ indexes draft-token positions within sampled blocks, excluding non-loss and anchor-token positions, and $T_{\mathrm{KD}}>0$ is the distillation temperature. This objective preserves the target model’s soft-label preferences and provides teacher-aligned candidate distributions for tree expansion.
64	3.4 Drafting and Verification
65	Parallel Tree Drafting.
66	An overview of the design is shown in Figure 3. At every decoding step $i$ , the causal draft head conditions on the hidden states $h_{x}^{o}$ of tokens that were verified and accepted in the previous step, and constructs a candidate tree with maximum draft depth $N$ , branching width $W$ , and total node budget $B$ . With one draft-head forward pass, we obtain logits for all draft depths and extract the top- $W$ candidate tokens at each depth. Tree expansion is then driven by a branch scoring function $s(\pi(v))$ , whose form can vary across implementations; we ablate different choices in Section 4.4. By default, we use accumulated draft log-probability for scoring: | |$s(\pi(v))=\sum_{u\in\pi(v)}\log r_{d(u)}\left(y_{u},\mid x,h_{x}^{o}\right),$  | |(7)
67	where where $d(u)$ is node depth and $r_{d}$ is the distribution produced at depth $d$ by the one-pass causal head. We then repeatedly pop the highest-scoring expandable node, expand it with up to $W$ children, and reinsert the children with updated scores until the budget is filled or no expandable node remains. This yields a candidate tree $\mathcal{T}(x)=\{\pi(v)\mid v\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathcal{T}}\}$ , where each path $\pi(v)$ is a speculative continuation; details are given in Algorithm 1.
68	Tree Verification.
69	After constructing the candidate tree $\mathcal{T}(x)$ , the target model $M_{p}$ verifies all tree nodes in parallel using tree attention. For any candidate branch $\pi(v)=y_{1:k}$ , the target distribution factorizes autoregressively in compliance with Equation 2.
70	The verifier then applies the speculative decoding acceptance rule along each candidate branch. For each draft token $y_{t}$ , we write the acceptance decision as | |$A_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\alpha_{t}),\qquad\alpha_{t}=\alpha\!\left(y_{t};\,q(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}),p(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\right),$  | |(8)
71	where $q$ is the draft distribution induced by $M_{q}$ , and $\alpha(\cdot)$ denotes the speculative verification rule. In standard non-greedy speculative sampling, this acceptance rule uses rejection sampling: | |$\alpha_{t}=\min\!\left(1,\,\frac{p(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{q(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}\right),$  | |(9)
72	with a target-model correction token sampled when rejection occurs (Leviathan et al., 2023). The accepted prefix length is $a=\max\left\{r\leq k:A_{t}=1,\ \forall t\leq r\right\}$ . In the greedy setting, $A_{t}$ becomes deterministic: a draft token is accepted if it matches the target model’s next-token prediction.
73	4 Experiments
74	4.1 Experiment Setup
75	Models and Datasets.
76	We evaluate JetSpec on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, covering both dense and MoE target models (Yang et al., 2025). Qwen3 supports both thinking and non-thinking modes, and we use the non-thinking mode throughout our main evaluation for efficient decoding. For training data, we curate 780K examples from the Nemotron Post-Training Dataset V2 (NVIDIA, 2025), including all available coding and math splits, random samples from STEM and chat splits, and 20K additional examples from CodeAlpaca (Chaudhary, 2023). For regenerated training sequences, we apply the corresponding chat template to each data type and continue generation with the target model. We evaluate on math benchmarks including GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021), and AIME25; coding benchmarks including HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), and LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2024); and open-ended conversational tasks including MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023). All ablation studies are conducted on the math split of Nemotron Post-Training Dataset V2.
77	Baselines and Training Settings.
78	We compare against EAGLE-3 and DFlash, two strong head-based speculative decoding baselines (Li et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). EAGLE-3 uses multi-layer feature fusion for direct token prediction, while DFlash uses a bidirectional block-parallel draft head to generate multiple draft tokens in one pass. DDTree (Ringel and Romano, 2026) constructs draft trees from DFlash’s per-position block-diffusion distributions using best-first tree expansion, but uses a pure block-diffusion head trained without loss weighting (Ringel and Romano, 2026). For fair comparison, we train JetSpec and all baselines on the same data mixture using a learning rate of $3\times 10^{-4}$ on 8 H100 GPUs. We also ablate DFlash-style loss weighting in Section 4.4; additional training details are provided in Appendix D.
79	Implementation Details.
80	For offline inference evaluation, we run experiments on 8 H100 or B200 GPUs. Unless otherwise specified, results in Table 2 use optimized Triton kernels for decoding. For serving-engine evaluation, we integrate JetSpec into vLLM (Appendix E), part of which involves tree verification with a custom SM90 paged FlashAttention kernel using NVIDIA CuTe DSL, extending the paged attention forward path with shared-memory tree-mask staging and tree-tail masking.
81	4.2 Results
82	We evaluate JetSpec under both greedy and non-greedy decoding settings in compliance with Equation 9. Evaluation results and comparisons with baselines are summarized in Table 1 and Table 2, and it shows JetSpec consistently outperforms tree-based baselines across all benchmarks.
83	Low-budget Regime.
84	Compared with the autoregressive drafting baseline EAGLE-3, JetSpec achieves substantially higher speedup at every reported budget by avoiding EAGLE-3’s higher sequential drafting overhead. At budget 16, DFlash and JetSpec perform nearly the same, suggesting that a short linear draft is already sufficient to cover many high-probability continuations. However, when increasing the budget to 32, JetSpec brings slight improvement, while DFlash often saturates or degrades. This indicates that JetSpec converts the additional draft budget into accepted tokens more effectively.

543	4.3 System Performance
544	We evaluate JetSpec in an end-to-end serving setting by integrating tree drafting and verification into vLLM. Serving performance depends not only on accepted length, but also on how the tree budget interacts with batching, verification overhead, memory traffic, and GPU occupancy. Larger budgets can reduce the number of target-model verification rounds, but also introduce higher draft-head and tree-verification cost, making the optimal budget load-dependent.
545	Budget Allocation.
546	Table 11 shows that larger tree budgets are most useful at small batch sizes. On H100 GPU at batch size 1, increasing the budget from 16 to 128 raises throughput from 224.0 to 553.3 TPS and end-to-end speedup from 1.75 $\times$ to 4.33 $\times$ . At batch size 16, a budget of 32 performs best at 3.81 $\times$ , while budget 128 drops to 2.80 $\times$ . This illustrates that larger budgets are most beneficial at low load, whereas heavier batching favors more moderate budgets.
547	Practical implication.
548	These results suggest that tree budgets should be selected according to serving load. Large budgets are preferable in low- to moderate-load regimes, where spare GPU capacity can be used to reduce decoding iterations. Under heavier load, smaller or moderate budgets may be more efficient by reducing per-step overhead and preserving batching efficiency. We evaluate static budget policies in this work and leave dynamic serving-time budget scheduling to future work.

The causal head is robust across $\gamma$ , while the diffusion head is sensitive to $\gamma$ and collapses at the endpoints (from $8.36\times$ at $\gamma=7$ to $5.46\times$ at $\gamma=0$ and $6.17\times$ at $\gamma=15$ ).

The actually-coherent “ are given that the” (target joint $-0.08$ ) sits at rank 3. The causal-head draft on the same prompt ranks “ are told that” first, with surrogate ${\approx}$ target joint (gap $-0.34$ ); tree verification accepts $6$ tokens from the causal-head tree but only $4$ from the diffusion-head tree (visualized in Figure 4 of Appendix A).

Full branch-level tables and the rank- $1$ gap distribution are in Appendix A.
655	4.5 Future Work
656	Several directions remain for future work. On the serving side, dynamic policies could adapt the draft budget to system load, while further systems optimization could reduce tree-verification-specific overheads, for example by using separate CUDA streams to overlap drafting with KV-block compaction. More flexible tree construction could allocate budget across depth and width based on branch confidence. Future work could also further exploit the causal structure of the draft model, for example through explicit causal factorization among draft tokens. Finally, hybrid policies could switch between linear and tree drafting for tasks where branching offers limited benefit.
657	5 Conclusion
658	We presented JetSpec, a causal parallel tree drafting framework for speculative decoding that jointly addresses the two factors limiting end-to-end speedup: drafting latency and accepted length. By causally coupling draftrepresentations while generating all depth-wise candidate distributions in a single low-cost pass, JetSpec makes tree construction better aligned with the target model’s autoregressive factorization. Across dense and MoE Qwen3 models and vLLM serving settings, JetSpec consistently turns larger draft budgets into higher wall-clock speedup, for MATH-500, reaching $9.64\times$ on Qwen3-8B, $9.45\times$ on Qwen3-30B-A3B, and up to 4.33 $\times$ serving throughput speedup on a single H100. These results show that causal coupling across draft positions improves long-budget speculative drafting while retaining one-pass efficiency.
659	AI Use Statement
660	In this work, we used generative AI tools to provide feedback on technical formulations and qualitative data analysis, we also used AI to help with method implementations. We have not used generative AI tools to generate synthetic datasets, develop theoretical models, assist in writing proofs, propose hypotheses, translate content, clean or reformat datasets, or interpret experimental results. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to edit and refine manuscript text for clarity and readability, suggest improvements to presentation and structure, and assist with literature search and verification. We reviewed all AI-assisted work and manually verified technical claims, citations, and suggested revisions against the original sources and our own experiments. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.
661	Reproducibility Statement
662	We provide detailed descriptions of the proposed method, training procedure, and system implementation to facilitate reproducibility. Appendix B specifies the parallel tree-drafting algorithm and scoring procedure; Appendix D reports the draft-head architecture, target-feature extraction, training data construction, optimization settings, and loss configurations; Appendix E describes the vLLM integration and optimized tree-verification implementation. We also provide the experimental code in the supplementary material.
663	Ethics Statement
664	All authors have read and adhere to the ICLR Code of Ethics. This work does not involve human subjects, sensitive personal data, or experiments with the potential to cause harm. No confidential or proprietary data were used. The methods and experiments were conducted in accordance with principles of research integrity, fairness, and transparency. Abstract
Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) by drafting multiple tokens and verifying them in parallel, but it faces a scaling limitation: increasing the draft budget improves speed only when acceptance remains high and drafting overhead stays low. This ceiling has been difficult to break because prior head-based SD methods face a causality-efficiency dilemma. Autoregressive drafters produce path-conditioned candidates that are effective for tree speculative decoding with higher acceptance length, but their drafting cost grows with tree depth. Bidirectional block-diffusion drafters generate all positions in one pass, but their branch-agnostic marginals can form individually plausible yet mutually inconsistent trees, wasting budget and reducing acceptance. We propose JetSpec, a head-based SD framework that combines one-forward drafting efficiency with causal information flow across draft representations. JetSpec trains a causal parallel draft head using fused hidden states from the frozen target model, producing causally coupled draft distributions whose scores better align with the target model’s autoregressive factorization. This enables JetSpec to convert larger draft budgets into longer accepted prefixes and higher end-to-end speedup. Across math, coding, and chat benchmarks on dense and MoE Qwen3 models, JetSpec consistently outperforms bidirectional-head and tree-based SD baselines. On H100 GPUs, JetSpec achieves up to $9.64\times$ speedup on MATH-500 and $4.58\times$ on open-ended conversational workloads, with further latency gains demonstrated through vLLM integration under realistic serving loads. Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/JetSpec. |
1 Introduction
Modern autoregressive (AR) Large Language Models (LLMs) operate under a simple yet costly bottleneck: decoding remains largely serial. This sequential generation process makes latency a major challenge when they are deployed in applications such as math (Wei et al., 2022; Zhu et al., 2025), coding (Deng et al., 2025; Jain et al., 2024) and other agentic reasoning tasks (Patil et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025), where models often perform long generations.
Existing approaches address this challenge by either incorporating multi-token prediction (MTP) during pre-training or mid-training (Gloeckle et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2026; AI, 2026; Xiaomi, 2026), or post-training methods that adapt pretrained LLMs into diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) at the costs of varying degrees of performance degradation (Zhao et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025). In contrast, applying speculative decoding (SD) at inference time to reduce generation latency while preserving quality (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023).
Among these techniques, SD stands out for its low adaptation cost and simplicity. On one hand, prior work shows that SD performance can be substantially improved through lightweight draft-model alignment, oftentimes less than 1B training tokens (Liu et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2024; Goel et al., 2024). On the other hand, head-based methods such as Medusa and EAGLE reduce deployment complexity by avoiding the conventional separate draft-target model setup (Cai et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b). More recent head-based methods such as EAGLE-3 (Li et al., 2025) and DFlash (Chen et al., 2026) continue to improve drafting quality and reducing drafting cost for better end-to-end acceleration. Despite these advances, head-based SD still faces a causality-efficiency dilemma. Autoregressive drafters such as EAGLE produce high-quality path-conditioned candidates but require sequential draft passes as tree depth grows. Bidirectional block-diffusion drafters such as DFlash produces drafts in one pass, but their branch-agnostic marginals can form individually plausible yet mutually inconsistent trees, wasting budget and reducing acceptance.
We propose JetSpec, a SD framework designed to break this causality–efficiency dilemma: JetSpec trains a causal parallel draft head to predict distributions for multiple draft depths in one forward pass while enforcing left-to-right information flow across draft-position hidden states. This produces causal depth-wise marginals that better reflect autoregressive continuation structure, enabling tree acceptance to scale more effectively with draft budget.
Empirically, JetSpec demonstrates significant efficiency gains. In the low-token-budget regime with 16 draft tokens, JetSpec achieves competitive end-to-end speedup.
In the high-token-budget regime with 256 draft tokens, JetSpec achieves strong gains, reaching $\tau=10.7$ and $9.5\times$ speedup on MATH-500, and remaining effective on MT-Bench with $\tau=5.9$ and over $4\times$ speedup. We further integrate JetSpec into industry-grade serving engine and evaluate it across batch sizes, where it consistently outperforms baselines under small to moderate serving loads, with especially strong gains on higher-end GPUs such as H100 and B200. These results highlight the practical potential of JetSpec for reducing decoding latency in serving.
Figure 1: 
End-to-end decoding speedup over standard autoregressive decoding on H100 GPUs across math, coding, and chat benchmarks. DFlash denotes the original block-parallel drafting method, DDTree is tree-based variant of DFlash, and JetSpec denotes our method. Both employ a tree budget of 256 tokens using Algorithm 1.
In a nutshell, our work makes the following contributions:
• 
We propose JetSpec, a paradigm designed to jointly optimize drafting cost and acceptance rate for speculative decoding. JetSpec trains a causal prediction head with parallel tree-drafting capability, enabling low-cost draft generation while preserving causal dependencies across draft-depth representations.
• 
We develop and evaluate tree-drafting algorithms that allow speculative decoding to better leverage additional decoding compute. By scaling the draft token budget, JetSpec achieves up to $\tau=10.7$ and more than $9.5\times$ end-to-end speedup.
• 
We integrate JetSpec into an industry-grade serving engine and evaluate it under realistic serving scenarios. JetSpec consistently outperforms baselines under small to moderate serving loads, highlighting its practical potential for reducing latency in real-world deployments.
2 Related Work
Speculative Decoding.
Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting tokens and verifying them with the target model (Leviathan et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2023). Its speedup depends on acceptance length and drafting cost. Prior work improves these factors via draft-target alignment (Zhou et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Goel et al., 2024), head-based drafters such as Medusa (Cai et al., 2024) and EAGLE (Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2025), or draft-free retrieval methods such as Prompt Lookup Decoding (Saxena, 2023), REST (He et al., 2024), PLD+ (Somasundaram et al., 2024), SAM Decoding (Hu et al., 2025b), and SuffixDecoding (Oliaro et al., 2024). While these methods reduce overhead, they often rely on semantic overlaps for retrieval, or repeated patterns. In contrast, JetSpec targets low-cost parallel drafting with a learned causal head that preserves branch-wise dependencies for high-acceptance tree verification.
Drafter Alignment.
Previous works train draft models or draft heads to better match the target model. Multi-token prediction objectives supervise future-token predictions during pretraining or midtraining (Gloeckle et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024), while post-training approaches use supervised fine-tuning, offline distillation, online distillation, or direct acceptance-rate optimization to improve agreement between draft and target distributions (Zhou et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Goel et al., 2024). These methods primarily improve the alignment term that controls acceptance rate. JetSpec is complementary: it trains the drafter not only to match the target model, but also to preserve directional structure for budgeted tree construction, so tree expansion uses causally coupled draft distributions rather than independent position marginals.
Parallel Decoding and Drafting.
Parallel decoding methods reduce latency by relaxing strict one-token-at-a-time generation. Self-speculative decoding drafts with early target-model layers and verifies with later layers (Elhoushi et al., 2024). Diffusion LLMs refine multiple tokens per iteration (Wu et al., 2025; Qian et al., 2026). Jacobi-style methods preserve causality by parallel fixed-point updates, with recent consistency distillation works improving convergence to autoregressive outputs (Fu et al., 2024; Kou et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025a). These methods increase tokens committed per forward, but are typically applied to the target model itself. DFlash generates multiple draft tokens in one block-parallel pass (Chen et al., 2026); DDTree further constructs trees from its bidirectional per-position distributions (Ringel and Romano, 2026), while Domino adds a lightweight sequential causal-correction head on top of a parallel drafter to condition later predictions on sampled earlier tokens (Huang et al., 2026); see Appendix B for a detailed comparison. In contrast, JetSpec introduces causal information flow directly within the parallel draft head, producing causally coupled depth-wise distributions for tree construction in a single forward pass.
3 JetSpec
3.1 Background
Scaling Bottlenecks in Speculative Decoding.
In speculative decoding (SD), a lightweight draft model $M_{q}$ proposes $N$ tokens, which are verified in parallel by the target model $M_{p}$  (Leviathan et al., 2023). The target accepts the longest prefix consistent with its predictions and resumes from the first rejected token. Let $\alpha$ denote the average acceptance rate and $c$ the per-step cost of $M_{q}$ relative to $M_{p}$ . Under the standard i.i.d. acceptance assumption, | |$\mathbb{E}[\#\mathrm{tokens}]=\frac{1-\alpha^{N+1}}{1-\alpha},\qquad\mathrm{Speedup}=\frac{1-\alpha^{N+1}}{(1-\alpha)(Nc+1)}.$  | |(1)
Thus, scaling to longer drafts requires both high acceptance $\alpha$ and low total drafting cost $Nc$ : as $N$ grows, even modest acceptance degradation or drafting overhead can offset the gains from parallel verification. Figure 2 illustrates this tradeoff.
(a) Typical SD ( $c=0.05$ ).
(b) Ultra low-cost SD ( $c=0.0005$ ).
Figure 2: 
Expected speculative decoding speedup scales as a function of draft length $\gamma$ , under different per-token drafting costs $c$ and acceptance rates $\alpha$ . Comparing the two panels shows that reducing $c$ substantially improves the scalability of speculative decoding with respect to $\gamma$ , and increasing $\alpha$ further amplifies this effect. The results highlight that pushing per-token drafting cost $c$ low and acceptance rate $\alpha$ high is critical for unlocking stronger scaling with longer draft lengths.
Existing work usually improves acceptance rate and drafting cost separately. To increase acceptance quality $\alpha$ , draft-model alignment methods improve agreement between $M_{q}$ and $M_{p}$  (Zhou et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024; Goel et al., 2024), while tree SD methods improve verification efficiency by expanding multiple candidate branches in parallel (Miao et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a). To reduce drafting cost $c$ , head-based methods avoid a separately deployed draft model (Cai et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b; Li et al., 2025); more recently, DFlash further reduces overhead through block-diffusion-style drafting, generating multiple draft tokens in a single draft pass (Chen et al., 2026) (see Appendix G). However, scaling to longer drafts requires simultaneously maintaining high $\alpha$ and low $c$ , motivating JetSpec to jointly improve acceptance rate and drafting efficiency.
3.2 Causal Parallel Drafting
Can We Realize Both Parallel Drafting and Tree SD?
A natural direction to co-optimize both aspects is to combine tree drafting for higher acceptance with parallel drafting for lower cost. However, existing parallel drafting methods such as DFlash can break the causal structure needed for effective tree construction: future-position marginals are produced without causal dependence on earlier draft positions, so high-probability marginals can compose into mutually inconsistent branches. JetSpec addresses this limitation with a causal parallel draft head that couples draft-depth representations left-to-right while preserving the efficiency of one-pass parallel prediction.
Why Causality Matters.
A tree inherently encodes a causal structure. Consider a draft tree rooted at the original prefix $x$ , where each node $v$ corresponds to a candidate token $y_{v}$ . Let $\pi(v)=(y_{v_{1}},\ldots,y_{v})$ denote the path from the root to $v$ , and $\pi_{<v}$ its ancestor tokens. Ideally, the distribution at each node should reflect its corresponding branch prefix. In contrast, a bidirectional parallel drafter allows each position to attend to representations from both earlier and later draft positions. It creates a mismatch between bidirectional draft representations and the causal structure required for tree construction.
Architecture.
JetSpec adopts a head-based drafting architecture, where a draft head can reuse intermediate features from the target model. Specifically, DFlash shows that a lightweight block-parallel draft head can reuse target-model hidden states and inject fused target-context features into the draft layers’ KV cache for strong target-model guidance (Chen et al., 2026). Building on this design, JetSpec introduces a causal parallel decoding head for tree drafting.
Given a prefix $x$ with fused target-model features $h_{x}^{o}$ , the draft head predicts logits for multiple future positions in parallel. Following standard speculative decoding notation, the target model defines an autoregressive distribution over a length- $k$ continuation: | |$p(y_{1:k}\mid x)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}p(y_{i}\mid x,y_{<i}).$  | |(2)
To introduce analogous directional dependencies into parallel drafting, we apply a causal attention mask across draft positions. Position $i$ may attend to the prefix features and earlier draft-position hidden states, but not to later positions. The mask and the masked attention at position $i$ are | |$B_{i,j}=\begin{cases}0,&j\leq i,\\
-\infty,&j>i,\end{cases},\qquad\mathrm{Attn}(Q_{i},K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{Q_{i}K^{\top}}{\sqrt{d}}+B_{i}\right)V,$  | |(3)
with prefix features visible to all draft positions. This allows all draft positions to be processed in parallel while enforcing directional information flow from earlier to later positions. Consequently, the distribution $r_{i}(\cdot\mid x,h_{x}^{o})$ at position $i$ is computed from a hidden representation that depends causally on earlier draft-position representations, rather than being produced independently across positions.
Figure 3: 
JetSpec design overview.
JetSpec extracts fused hidden features from the frozen target model and conditions a causal-parallel draft head to generate high-quality candidate trees in one forward pass.
The causal mask induces directional dependencies across draft-position representations. Let $h_{i}^{q}$ denote the draft-head hidden state at position $i$ . Then | |$h_{i}^{q}=M_{q}\!\left(x,h_{x}^{o},h_{<i}^{q}\right),\qquad q_{i}=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(Wh_{i}^{q}\right),$  | |(4)
where $h_{<i}^{q}$ denotes earlier draft-position representations and $q_{i}$ the token distribution at position $i$ . Although all positions are predicted in parallel, each position causally incorporates earlier representations, introducing directional dependencies for tree drafting.
3.3 Training
Data Preparation.
We train the draft head on target-aligned sequences, obtained either from the training corpus, as in multi-token prediction (Gloeckle et al., 2024; DeepSeek-AI, 2024), or from
continuations regenerated by the target model (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2026). Given a sequence $(x,y_{1:k})$ , we sample anchor positions and, at each anchor, construct a length- $N$ training block of $N$ consecutive future positions. The draft head predicts these $N$ positions in parallel under a block-causal mask, matching the per-position teacher logits produced by the target model on the same ground-truth prefix.
Distillation Loss.
We train the draft head with a soft-label distillation objective so that the draft distribution preserves the target model’s relative preferences across multiple plausible continuations. Among distillation objectives, forward KL encourages the draft distribution to cover the target model’s probability mass, preserving soft-label information beyond the top prediction. Reverse KL, in contrast, is more mode-seeking and can concentrate probability on high-confidence teacher modes (Gu et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2024). We find this matters in practice (Section 4): reverse KL underperforms substantially, while forward KL slightly outperforms hard-label SFT. We therefore adopt forward KL by default, and present the loss in this form below.
For each active draft position $m$ , let $z_{q}^{(m)}$ and $z_{p}^{(m)}$ denote the draft and target logits over the vocabulary $\mathcal{V}$ . We define temperature-normalized distributions
 $\tilde{q}^{(m)}=\mathrm{softmax}(z_{q}^{(m)}/T_{\mathrm{KD}})$ 
and
 $\tilde{p}^{(m)}=\mathrm{softmax}(z_{p}^{(m)}/T_{\mathrm{KD}})$ , and minimize the forward KL | |$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FKL}}^{(m)}=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(\tilde{p}^{(m)}\,\middle\|\,\tilde{q}^{(m)}\right).$  | |(5)
The final objective is computed over all active draft-token positions induced from the training sequence and normalized by the active-position mask (see Appendix D for details): | |$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{train}}=T_{\mathrm{KD}}^{2}\frac{\sum_{m}w_{m}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FKL}}^{(m)}}{\sum_{m}w_{m}},$  | |(6)
where $m$ indexes draft-token positions within sampled blocks, excluding non-loss and anchor-token positions, and $T_{\mathrm{KD}}>0$ is the distillation temperature. This objective preserves the target model’s soft-label preferences and provides teacher-aligned candidate distributions for tree expansion.
3.4 Drafting and Verification
Parallel Tree Drafting.
An overview of the design is shown in Figure 3. At every decoding step $i$ , the causal draft head conditions on the hidden states $h_{x}^{o}$ of tokens that were verified and accepted in the previous step, and constructs a candidate tree with maximum draft depth $N$ , branching width $W$ , and total node budget $B$ . With one draft-head forward pass, we obtain logits for all draft depths and extract the top- $W$ candidate tokens at each depth. Tree expansion is then driven by a branch scoring function $s(\pi(v))$ , whose form can vary across implementations; we ablate different choices in Section 4.4. By default, we use accumulated draft log-probability for scoring: | |$s(\pi(v))=\sum_{u\in\pi(v)}\log r_{d(u)}\left(y_{u},\mid x,h_{x}^{o}\right),$  | |(7)
where where $d(u)$ is node depth and $r_{d}$ is the distribution produced at depth $d$ by the one-pass causal head. We then repeatedly pop the highest-scoring expandable node, expand it with up to $W$ children, and reinsert the children with updated scores until the budget is filled or no expandable node remains. This yields a candidate tree $\mathcal{T}(x)=\{\pi(v)\mid v\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathcal{T}}\}$ , where each path $\pi(v)$ is a speculative continuation; details are given in Algorithm 1.
Tree Verification.
After constructing the candidate tree $\mathcal{T}(x)$ , the target model $M_{p}$ verifies all tree nodes in parallel using tree attention. For any candidate branch $\pi(v)=y_{1:k}$ , the target distribution factorizes autoregressively in compliance with Equation 2.
The verifier then applies the speculative decoding acceptance rule along each candidate branch. For each draft token $y_{t}$ , we write the acceptance decision as | |$A_{t}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\alpha_{t}),\qquad\alpha_{t}=\alpha\!\left(y_{t};\,q(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}),p(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\right),$  | |(8)
where $q$ is the draft distribution induced by $M_{q}$ , and $\alpha(\cdot)$ denotes the speculative verification rule. In standard non-greedy speculative sampling, this acceptance rule uses rejection sampling: | |$\alpha_{t}=\min\!\left(1,\,\frac{p(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}{q(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})}\right),$  | |(9)
with a target-model correction token sampled when rejection occurs (Leviathan et al., 2023). The accepted prefix length is $a=\max\left\{r\leq k:A_{t}=1,\ \forall t\leq r\right\}$ . In the greedy setting, $A_{t}$ becomes deterministic: a draft token is accepted if it matches the target model’s next-token prediction.
4 Experiments
4.1 Experiment Setup
Models and Datasets.
We evaluate JetSpec on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B, covering both dense and MoE target models (Yang et al., 2025). Qwen3 supports both thinking and non-thinking modes, and we use the non-thinking mode throughout our main evaluation for efficient decoding. For training data, we curate 780K examples from the Nemotron Post-Training Dataset V2 (NVIDIA, 2025), including all available coding and math splits, random samples from STEM and chat splits, and 20K additional examples from CodeAlpaca (Chaudhary, 2023). For regenerated training sequences, we apply the corresponding chat template to each data type and continue generation with the target model. We evaluate on math benchmarks including GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021), and AIME25; coding benchmarks including HumanEval (Chen et al., 2021), MBPP (Austin et al., 2021), and LiveCodeBench (Jain et al., 2024); and open-ended conversational tasks including MT-Bench (Zheng et al., 2023). All ablation studies are conducted on the math split of Nemotron Post-Training Dataset V2.
Baselines and Training Settings.
We compare against EAGLE-3 and DFlash, two strong head-based speculative decoding baselines (Li et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026). EAGLE-3 uses multi-layer feature fusion for direct token prediction, while DFlash uses a bidirectional block-parallel draft head to generate multiple draft tokens in one pass. DDTree (Ringel and Romano, 2026) constructs draft trees from DFlash’s per-position block-diffusion distributions using best-first tree expansion, but uses a pure block-diffusion head trained without loss weighting (Ringel and Romano, 2026). For fair comparison, we train JetSpec and all baselines on the same data mixture using a learning rate of $3\times 10^{-4}$ on 8 H100 GPUs. We also ablate DFlash-style loss weighting in Section 4.4; additional training details are provided in Appendix D.
Implementation Details.
For offline inference evaluation, we run experiments on 8 H100 or B200 GPUs. Unless otherwise specified, results in Table 2 use optimized Triton kernels for decoding. For serving-engine evaluation, we integrate JetSpec into vLLM (Appendix E), part of which involves tree verification with a custom SM90 paged FlashAttention kernel using NVIDIA CuTe DSL, extending the paged attention forward path with shared-memory tree-mask staging and tree-tail masking.
4.2 Results
We evaluate JetSpec under both greedy and non-greedy decoding settings in compliance with Equation 9. Evaluation results and comparisons with baselines are summarized in Table 1 and Table 2, and it shows JetSpec consistently outperforms tree-based baselines across all benchmarks.
Low-budget Regime.
Compared with the autoregressive drafting baseline EAGLE-3, JetSpec achieves substantially higher speedup at every reported budget by avoiding EAGLE-3’s higher sequential drafting overhead. 4.3 System Performance
We evaluate JetSpec in an end-to-end serving setting by integrating tree drafting and verification into vLLM. Serving performance depends not only on accepted length, but also on how the tree budget interacts with batching, verification overhead, memory traffic, and GPU occupancy. Larger budgets can reduce the number of target-model verification rounds, but also introduce higher draft-head and tree-verification cost, making the optimal budget load-dependent.
Budget Allocation.
Table 11 shows that larger tree budgets are most useful at small batch sizes. On H100 GPU at batch size 1, increasing the budget from 16 to 128 raises throughput from 224.0 to 553.3 TPS and end-to-end speedup from 1.75 $\times$ to 4.33 $\times$ . At batch size 16, a budget of 32 performs best at 3.81 $\times$ , while budget 128 drops to 2.80 $\times$ . This illustrates that larger budgets are most beneficial at low load, whereas heavier batching favors more moderate budgets.
Practical implication.
These results suggest that tree budgets should be selected according to serving load. Large budgets are preferable in low- to moderate-load regimes, where spare GPU capacity can be used to reduce decoding iterations. Under heavier load, smaller or moderate budgets may be more efficient by reducing per-step overhead and preserving batching efficiency. We evaluate static budget policies in this work and leave dynamic serving-time budget scheduling to future work.

4.4.2 Tree Drafting with Diffusion Head
Table 7: Architecture and $\gamma$ ablation on MATH-500 with JetSpec at LR $3{\times}10^{-4}$ with forward-KL distillation. We report speedup and average accepted length $\tau$ . |Head |$\gamma=0$  |$\gamma=3$  |$\gamma=7$  |$\gamma=15$  |Speedup |$\tau$  |Speedup |$\tau$  |Speedup |$\tau$  |Speedup |$\tau$  |Causal |8.29 |9.81 |8.50 |10.00 |8.40 |9.99 |8.41 |9.96 |Diffusion |5.46 |6.45 |8.16 |9.65 |8.36 |9.72 |6.17 |7.19
Table 7 compares causal and diffusion heads under different choices of $\gamma$ , the parameter that controls how aggressively the DFlash training objective downweights per-position loss at positions far from each anchor token. Specifically, position $i$ within a block contributes to the training loss with weight $w_{i}=\exp\!\left(-\max(i-i_{\mathrm{anchor}},\,0)/\gamma\right)$ , where $\gamma=0$ is interpreted as the limit of uniform per-position weighting (no decay). The causal head is robust across $\gamma$ , while the diffusion head is sensitive to $\gamma$ and collapses at the endpoints (from $8.36\times$ at $\gamma=7$ to $5.46\times$ at $\gamma=0$ and $6.17\times$ at $\gamma=15$ ).
A failure example.
On MATH-500 prompt $0$ at decode step $0$ , the diffusion-head draft ( $\gamma=0$ ) ranks “ given told that” first in its tree, with cumulative draft surrogate $\sum_{i}\log r_{i}=-3.76$ but cumulative target conditional $\sum_{i}\log p(y_{i}\mid x,\pi_{<v_{i}})=-63.32$ nats: the branch combines two mutually exclusive openers, exemplifying the failure mode discussed in Section 3.2. The actually-coherent “ are given that the” (target joint $-0.08$ ) sits at rank 3. The causal-head draft on the same prompt ranks “ are told that” first, with surrogate ${\approx}$ target joint (gap $-0.34$ ); tree verification accepts $6$ tokens from the causal-head tree but only $4$ from the diffusion-head tree (visualized in Figure 4 of Appendix A).
Aggregate generalization.
Across MATH-500 prompts $0$ – $49$ , the diffusion-head’s rank- $1$ gap exceeds the causal-head’s on $92\%$ of prompts, with a median $5\times$ larger ( $+62.81$ vs. $+12.36$ nats); the mean per-step accepted-token ratio is $1.95\times$ , closely matching the macroscopic $1.52\times$ speedup ratio in Table 7. Full branch-level tables and the rank- $1$ gap distribution are in Appendix A.
4.5 Future Work
Several directions remain for future work. On the serving side, dynamic policies could adapt the draft budget to system load, while further systems optimization could reduce tree-verification-specific overheads, for example by using separate CUDA streams to overlap drafting with KV-block compaction. More flexible tree construction could allocate budget across depth and width based on branch confidence. Future work could also further exploit the causal structure of the draft model, for example through explicit causal factorization among draft tokens. Finally, hybrid policies could switch between linear and tree drafting for tasks where branching offers limited benefit.
5 Conclusion
We presented JetSpec, a causal parallel tree drafting framework for speculative decoding that jointly addresses the two factors limiting end-to-end speedup: drafting latency and accepted length. By causally coupling draftrepresentations while generating all depth-wise candidate distributions in a single low-cost pass, JetSpec makes tree construction better aligned with the target model’s autoregressive factorization. Across dense and MoE Qwen3 models and vLLM serving settings, JetSpec consistently turns larger draft budgets into higher wall-clock speedup, for MATH-500, reaching $9.64\times$ on Qwen3-8B, $9.45\times$ on Qwen3-30B-A3B, and up to 4.33 $\times$ serving throughput speedup on a single H100. These results show that causal coupling across draft positions improves long-budget speculative drafting while retaining one-pass efficiency.

We have not used generative AI tools to generate synthetic datasets, develop theoretical models, assist in writing proofs, propose hypotheses, translate content, clean or reformat datasets, or interpret experimental results. We provide detailed descriptions of the proposed method, training procedure, and system implementation to facilitate reproducibility. Appendix B specifies the parallel tree-drafting algorithm and scoring procedure; Appendix D reports the draft-head architecture, target-feature extraction, training data construction, optimization settings, and loss configurations; Appendix E describes the vLLM integration and optimized tree-verification implementation. We also provide the experimental code in the supplementary material.

content.content: Appendix B Tree-Drafting Algorithm Details Algorithm 1 describes how JetSpec constructs a candidate tree under a fixed node budget. Starting from the root prefix $x$ , the algorithm maintains a priority queue of expandable nodes ranked by a branch scoring function $\mathrm{Score}(\cdot)$ . At each iteration, it expands the highest-scoring node by adding up to $W$ children at the next depth, unless the node has already reached the maximum draft depth $N$ . Each new child is inserted back into the queue with its updated path score, and the process continues until the total node budget $B$ is exhausted. The returned tree $\mathcal{T}(x)$ therefore contains the highest-scoring candidate branches according to the chosen scoring rule.
